A demonstration of this approach is provided, showcasing its application to Michigan primary election data. Furthermore, a comparison is made between the iOCR approach and a traditional OCR method, highlighting the effectiveness of iOCR in accurately processing ballot data.

In deep learning models, overparameterization is often paired with regularization to prevent overfitting. This study explores how these factors interact in a time series learning context, investigating how a linear model performs when trained on a limited dataset with an excess of parameters. To achieve this, a novel approach was developed, involving the random splitting of data into training and validation sets at each time step. This method enabled assessment of overfitting reduction due to data limitation alone, separated from other factors such as regularization and optimization processes. With this approach, a significant decrease in overfitting was observed when comparing models trained on longer time series periods with those trained on shorter periods, despite having more parameters. Conversely, no further improvement was found in model accuracy when moving from a highly limited to a more extensive time series dataset. These findings suggest that overparameterization alone may provide a similar overfitting reduction benefit to that achieved with strong model assumptions in a time series context, particularly when learning from a limited continuous signal.

Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper showcases a novel deep learning architecture, centered on a comprehensive attention mechanism within a bidirectional neural network. This innovative design deviates from conventional attention-based models that often apply complicated memory modules and limited contextual information, whereas our proposed framework leverages contextual information from both distant and nearby past and future input elements. Through experimental evaluations on the CHIME-3 dataset, our model demonstrates superior performance compared to established deep learning and attention-based methods.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study also demonstrates that the resonant frequency-based attack can target multiple rooms simultaneously. Furthermore, we were able to successfully test this technique at a fully functional FDA-approved NPR located within a biomedical facility. Our research offers several measures that could mitigate this type of attack.

A key factor in microgrid operations is the capacity to store energy, but it also introduces new risks due to potential inefficiencies in market mechanisms. This study analyzes how risk-averse market participants self-allocate energy storage to maximize their expected rewards, taking into account the uncertainty of reward outcomes. We establish conditions for continuous and integer storage options that guarantee optimal solutions can be found efficiently and explore the implications of these results for market design. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the performance of self-allocated storage options in simulated markets. This research provides a foundation for advancing theory and practical applications in its field.

In quantum systems, superpositions of electronic states rapidly evolve, 
within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the temporal evolution 
of core electrons over several femtoseconds. A theoretical model accounting for 
electronic and nuclear motion as well as the internal field within the molecule 
provides a clear understanding of experimental findings. It shows that, due to the 
vibrational state, electronic waves interfere either constructively or destructively, 
resulting in varying intensity levels over time as observed in our results.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds.

Deep learning models have seen a significant boost in performance when trained on a large, diverse range of visual data. However, creating large, high-quality training datasets for new visual classification tasks is a challenging task. Researchers have made progress in scaling down existing datasets through selective re-labeling, but the effectiveness of these methods has not been thoroughly evaluated yet. This paper presents the results of applying dynamic learning methods to large, partially labeled datasets, containing around 200 categories from the ImageNet dataset. Dynamic learning involves creating multiple narrow classes within each of the broader categories and optimizing the model to focus on these distinct regions. When using a self-supervised pre-training method, dynamic learning delivers around 5% improvement in top-1 accuracy with around 50 times fewer labeled data, around 10% better than traditional supervised learning. Additionally, dynamic learning demonstrates around 6% improvement in top-1 accuracy when using a fully labeled dataset of around 150 categories.

This work offers a novel perspective on the concept of an algebraic multiplicity, which is a key element in Henri Cartan's theorem that links the algebraic and geometric multiplicities of a point to the singularity index of a map. By incorporating discrete geometric data, the multiplicity can be viewed as a measure of a point's local dimension within the complex plane. This approach enables the creation of bi-dimensional spectra, which provide a more comprehensive understanding of a map's local structure. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the versatility of this approach across multiple dimensional contexts.

We suggest creating pairs of correlated bosonic states within a specific type of atomic system that includes dipolar atoms connected to an optical cavity. This model can be used to develop an optical homodyne measurement technique that accurately detects the phase of a light field. The pair creation process is fueled by the interaction between two closely spaced atomic transitions and is controlled through laser intensity. By manipulating this control, we can generate both squeezed states and, for the first time, a novel state that is simultaneously paired and correlated with an optical state. This latter state has potential applications in testing quantum operations with large dipolar atoms.

Researchers who utilize silicon-based infrastructure for quantum computing need to model the behavior of phosphorus atoms, which serve as quantum bits, due to their potential to store and manipulate data. To accomplish this, a method of simulation has been developed by applying a valley-degenerate effective mass approach. This approach allows for the examination of donor atoms' behavior under applied magnetic fields by considering the interactions between valence and conduction bands in silicon. By utilizing a large unit cell and an efficient algorithm for the calculation of the band structure, this method can simulate the behavior of up to three phosphorus atoms placed strategically in silicon. The results of these simulations reveal the necessity for a precise understanding of the relationship between donor atoms' configuration and the behavior of conduction electrons. Specifically, in situations where the distance between donor atoms is comparable to the size of the orbital surrounding each individual donor, a more intricate analysis is required. By accounting for the interactions between these orbitals, significant improvements can be made to the accuracy of quantum operations such as gate construction. Furthermore, in addition to modeling single quantum bits, this method also enables the exploration of more complex quantum applications, such as the construction of quantum gates for multiple bits at once.

Our investigation focuses on the conductance of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by the four-fold degenerate Dirac points. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a singular peak appears in the conductance at its beginning, which correlates with the heavy mass associated with the in-plane motion of Dirac fermions. This peak vanishes in larger samples, and instead, the conductance is defined by the smaller light mass, which represents the motion perpendicular to the quantum well. This happens because the larger samples experience significant transverse resistance due to the large distance between the opposing contacts. As a result, electrons experience significant lateral scattering, which forces them to move perpendicular to the quantum well and accelerate quickly in that direction. This forces the in-plane motion to slow down and eventually disappear, revealing the conductance properties induced by the minimal energy gap near the Dirac points.

Roadside safety has been a pressing concern for mobile communication systems, which are prone to catastrophic failures due to their long distance between base stations and the movement of vehicles. To address this issue, a fifth-generation mobile communication system with advanced capabilities can provide stable connections even in challenging environments of road intersections and bridges; however, developing an accurate performance assessment method for these areas remains a difficulty. In this study, a novel approach based on adaptive cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (ACNOMA) protocol is introduced, and the complex problems of vehicle flow modeling and signal propagation are simplified using the probability-generating function technique and the concept of effective communication distance. By establishing a practical model of network performance, the effects of various variables on end-to-end system performance are analyzed, and optimal parameter values are determined through optimization methods. The research found that ACNOMA-based systems outperform traditional CO-NOMA systems when it comes to end-to-end system performance, and that increasing the number of vehicles in the flow decreases overall system performance.

In our proposed approach, we develop a mathematical model that schedules operations for an edge computing system using Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing. By modeling interference and task processing times, we formulate an optimization problem to maximize edge computing performance. This optimization problem is nonconvex, making it challenging to find a global optimum. To address this, we modify the problem into a convex optimization problem by defining a new variable and formulating the problem in a way that involves the Schur Complement. This modification enables us to apply convex optimization techniques, such as the Newton-Raphson method, to find an optimal solution. Furthermore, we prove that our approach converges to an optimal solution under certain conditions. To validate our approach, we develop an algorithm based on modified game-theoretic reasoning and demonstrate its convergence. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between our approach and a fully optimal solution, as well as the effects of computing accuracy on system performance.

An analysis of a Hall anomaly in YBCO has been successfully replicated by incorporating the effects of moving vacancies in a fixed lattice of vortices, and their interaction is quantified using new parameters that are determined from BSCCO thin-film data. This model highlights the significance of vacancies in understanding Hall anomaly, and it reveals that the predicted vortex-vacancy binding energy and mobility match with previously measured values in YBCO and BSCCO. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the predicted density of vacancies also aligns with expected values, particularly in YBCO, and it shows that the predicted vacancy contribution to the normal density and the resulting shift in the Hall resistance are in line with measured values in BSCCO. Additionally, this model demonstrates that the predicted increase in the normal density and the resulting shift in the Hall resistance in YBCO can be explained by existing data, and it shows that the predicted vortex-vacancy binding energy and mobility can be explained by measuring the time-dependent resistance in YBCO.

Using experimental data from magnetic measurements in the Ising model's critical region, researchers previously found a consistent fixed point characteristic for all moments of the order parameter. To further investigate this phenomenon, new analysis is presented for the moments of the order parameter in the Ising model's critical region, primarily utilizing correlation functions obtained from Monte Carlo simulations in the universality class of the 3D Ising model. The calculations yield explicit, closed-form expressions for the moments of the order parameter, from which a consistent fixed point behavior can be determined. Notably, this fixed point characterizes not only the moments of the order parameter but also the distribution of the order parameter. In addition, new estimates are derived for key critical exponents in the 3D Ising model.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares that generate a type of subfactor known as a factor is well-known. However, when the subfactor is not a factor, the characterization becomes more complex and involves additional criteria. In this research, the fundamental properties of a subfactor's index and depth are characterized in terms of its associated square, under specific conditions. Specifically, certain conditions on the square's dimension and the behavior of its morphism and unitary operator are met. Although the requirement for the subfactor's depth to be two may seem restrictive, it is demonstrated that this restriction is inevitable. The principles established in this research are relevant to both the compact interval [0,4] and the rational number 4/3.

In this work, we examine the capability of Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HamNNs) to acquire derivative information, which is a crucial aspect for their potential application in solving ordinary and partial differential equations through the Hamiltonian Neural Network method we proposed earlier. However, our research indicates that using this approach leads to the duplication of signal information, resulting in unnecessary computation and potential errors. To address this issue, we suggest modifying HamNNs to extract both the signal and derivative from a single latent variable, which significantly enhances their performance. Additionally, we find that incorporating noise into the derivative signal improves the training convergence rate. Our proposed architecture, which we term the Hamiltonian Neural Network with noise (HamNN-n), achieves the best-in-class accuracy for benchmark tasks including the inverse problem and the heat equation, surpassing the limitations of the original HamNN. Our code is openly accessible on MMFF at https://mmff.org competitions/, where further details can be found.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing users' confidence in it. A proposed framework establishes a collaborative relationship between computing experts and human evaluators to refine a machine learning model's reliability. This involves creating a scoring system to assess the model's performance based on human feedback, as well as a method to boost performance by selectively adding diverse data. The framework is designed to be adaptable to various types of data and classification algorithms. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted a series of tests using a dataset from the image classification category. The results showed that, even in the presence of significant biases in the data, the framework is capable of significantly reducing classification errors. Additionally, we discovered that the technique of selective data augmentation is an important factor in achieving these results.

Detecting prohibited items in an x-ray image of luggage is crucial for ensuring public safety. However, the difficulty of these images makes it challenging for artificial intelligence to determine prohibited items. For instance, certain items like drugs have contrasting colors, while others like explosives and firearms are missing in many training datasets. Furthermore, many prohibited items appear similar to everyday objects in x-ray images. On top of that, lung diseases and anomalous blood patterns can appear as prohibited items or hide prohibited items in x-ray images. Consequently, creating a reliable artificial intelligence system for detecting prohibited items in x-ray images requires addressing several challenges. So far, research on this topic has been limited by the quality of the data used for training and the lack of diversity in the items being detected. For instance, the LUNA dataset, which is commonly used for training and evaluating artificial intelligence systems for detecting lung diseases, also contains x-ray images of lung tissues as well as entire lung images. Nevertheless, lung diseases can manifest differently in x-ray images of lung tissues and entire lung images. On the other hand, the LUNA dataset does not contain diversity in the items being detected. For example, it does not contain images of drugs, explosives, or firearms. Furthermore, the names of the classes being predicted are confusingly similar to the names of lung diseases. Consequently, creating a reliable artificial intelligence system for detecting prohibited items in x-ray images requires addressing several challenges. Therefore, we introduce a new benchmark dataset called the XRay

We introduce a novel quantum invariant, dubbed the 'Category Norm', for links in a thickened torus. This invariant is constructed from the category grading in a modified version of the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus, specifically using the volume hypothesis. It's notable for being a multipartition function that varies with angle, similar to the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant but with an essential difference. Furthermore, we prove that this invariant shares many properties with the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant but falls short of being an exact functor due to not retain the properties of convolution or multiplication. Despite this, it does retain the properties of being tamely ramified and having asymptotic behavior at infinity. Moreover, we prove that it meets the volume hypothesis and that its values lie within the range of nonnegative integers, with some values reaching infinity. Additionally, we observe that it exhibits periodic behavior under 32nd root transformations, similar to the Witten-Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant but with a different shift.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine contextual information and learn neural models.  However, the challenge remains that many words possess limited context due to the sparse nature of annotated data, which hinders the training of WSD models.  To address this issue, the paper proposes contextual augmentation techniques, along with a novel framework called Context-gloss Enhancer (CgE) to enhance the context of ambiguous words by combining the meanings of related words (hypernyms and hyponyms) expressed in natural language.  The CgE framework includes three specific context augmentation strategies: Hypernym Gloss Augmentation (HGA), Hyponym Gloss Insertion (HGI), and Cycle-regulated Context Refining (CCR), which are systematically evaluated to achieve the current state-of-the-art performance on the WordSenseSpace (WSS) dataset.

This paper formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a specific regularization. Additionally, it presents related, regularization-dependent integral expressions of the gamma function.

This paper investigates top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions at 13 TeV and above, using the medium-modified parton fragmentation fragmenting into $b$-tagged jets. We demonstrate the significance of detecting top quark production beyond purely muonic decay modes, considering experimental acceptances and primary and secondary particle lists. Furthermore, we establish minimum requirements for $W$ boson reconstruction, depending on collision energy and medium properties. If the modification of parton fragmentation due to the medium is insufficient, detection in proton-nucleus collisions may be challenging than in heavy-ion collisions. However, if the medium impact on parton fragmentation is significant, top quark production can be readily identified with $S/$$N\sim 3-5$ in $pp$ collisions at 13 TeV and above, or with $S/$$N\sim 5-7$ in $pp$ collisions at 8 TeV.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL tasks, specifically schema and value prediction, and introduces a novel framework to address these elements across different datasets. The proposed approach incorporates multiple techniques to enhance the interpretation of text, including joint predictions, auxiliary tasks, and domain adaptation. Notably, the framework makes several significant contributions to the field, including the introduction of a new dataset, the development of a scalable model architecture, and the proof that auxiliary tasks and cross-domain adaptation can significantly improve text-to-SQL performance.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy (DP) on networks, focusing on boosting the accuracy of frequency estimates for sensitive network data, specifically on WSNs. The first section outlines the theoretical foundations of DP and its various privacy guarantees. The second section explores DP applications related to frequency predictions. The third section investigates DP protocols for sensing multiple frequencies in WSNs; particularly, the section discusses recent approaches using DP for broad spectrum sensing in such environments. The fourth section discusses other DP networks, encompassing time-series sensing, healthcare, and social network applications. The fifth section presents challenges, potential future areas of research, and practical difficulties in this field. The authors also contribute a novel framework integrating DP with frequency estimation in general network settings, alongside a novel decoding method for enhancing the accuracy of frequency estimates using a small network of sensors.

The vast image database and technological advancements in the Euclid mission will significantly impact image analysis methods, making it essential to incorporate machine learning and multi-band information into its scientific objectives. As a result, traditional methods used for source extraction and photometry will need modification to accommodate these changes. For example, the formation of catalogues around the satellite's observing patterns and potential issues with satellite system noises become crucial considerations. Furthermore, the mission's extensive data holdings create opportunities for statistical analysis beyond its core objectives, potentially leading to the discovery of rare phenomena otherwise overlooked due to their intensity.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create Bezier curves, we define the parameters of a virtual world in which the vehicle can operate. To identify potential issues with these systems, we develop an optimization algorithm that refines the road network and vehicle path in search of areas that cause the vehicle to stray from its intended course. Through this approach, we can efficiently create realistic scenarios that pose a challenge to autonomous lane-keeping systems. To support our method, we also present a practical application of our search algorithm, demonstrating its capability to improve the performance of a lane-following controller.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist.

Researchers have successfully used quantum hydrodynamics to study non-equilibrium situations for interacting Bose gases, albeit within a limited framework that relies on hydrodynamics' basic assumptions. A new approach uses the method of phase-space quantum field theory in curved spacetime to generate a random quantum hydrodynamic description, capable of addressing more complex situations. This approach enables the investigation of a gas's dynamical properties through the hydrodynamic equation, by first determining the quadratic part of the boson's self-energy in momentum and frequency, and then incorporating this self-energy into the quantum hydrodynamic equation. In a situation resembling a weakly interacting gas close to a symmetry-breaking transition, another quantum field theory framework yields comparable results, but the random quantum hydrodynamics approach provides a more comprehensive explanation, involving both local order and non-local modes. The interplay between these modes leads to the local mode's unstable growth induced by the non-local mode's interaction, and the possibility of the gas transitioning to a state with greater order over time. Additionally, the random quantum hydrodynamics approach predicts that local modes may exhibit damped growth instead of instability, depending on an initial condition.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

The theory of edge localized modes (ELMs) is challenged by the appearance of palm tree modes (PTMs) in inertial confinement plasmas on the JET tokamak. PTMs are a phenomenon where magnetic fluctuations cause a reduction in the edge current, leading to a disruption of the plasma, and PTMs occur concurrently with low-hazard ELMs. A newly proposed model suggests that the generation of PTMs is a result of the interaction between magnetic fluctuations and edge particles that are transferred to the plasma interior, and this model is tested for accuracy using data from the ICRF reflectometer on JET. Our findings support the model's prediction that the primary driver of PTMs is the transfer of particles by edge flows, and that the associated change in the current can be as significant as 20 A. This understanding has implications for the prediction of dangerous ELMs, and it is proposed that the relationship between ELMs and PTMs could provide valuable insights into the physics of magnetic fluctuations in plasmas.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for mobile robots moving at constant speeds in a static environment, addressing this issue using dynamic vortex potential fields in a collaborative and fundamental approach. By applying this method, a scalable and efficient collision avoidance system is implemented for robots with different speeds. In addition, simulations and practical applications validate the effectiveness of this strategy.

Consider a long sequence of letters generated from an underlying source model, which comprises multiple components including a word pattern source and word pattern estimates. Assuming certain regularity conditions are met, we establish two types of large deviation principles for estimating the frequency of occurrence of specific patterns within these sequences. The first principle applies when the frequency estimate is based on a single realisation of the sequence, yielding an exponential average large deviation bound that incorporates dependencies between letters. The second principle arises when frequency estimates are compared across distinct source models, resulting in an exponential large deviation bound that accounts for both discrepancies between models and variations between letters. These principles have implications for both statistical inference and coding tasks.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, the IRS has been explored in conjunction with various wireless technologies, including 5G radar systems. This paper investigates the potential of the IRS to enhance target parameter estimation in radar applications. To achieve this, a dual-target scenario radar environment was simulated and target parameter estimation was performed with and without an IRS. Results showed that an IRS can significantly improve target parameter estimation by facilitating higher accuracy rates, outperforming conventional approaches by up to 90%. Furthermore, the characteristics of the proposed IRS method were examined in detail.

Fuzzers are widely used testing tools for robustness, exploiting innocent inputs to elicit harmful responses from sensitive systems. Their success stems from a few well-chosen mutation strategies, often hidden from view, as they simply present polished inputs to targets. To achieve their goal, fuzzers typically employ two key techniques: matching and merging. During matching, incoming data is compared to a stored standard, while merging involves combining the two to create new samples. Although fuzzers seem straightforward, their inner workings are not well understood, as the community lacks a universal language to discuss them. To address this gap, we propose a formal framework for comparing and modifying testing datasets. This framework enables the clear definition of mutation strategies, as well as the systematic analysis of fusion strategies. Furthermore, it provides a platform for comparing and modifying data, including the modification of static data. Through our framework, we are able to derive several theoretical advantages of different mutation strategies and demonstrate its practical applications with the well-known Sulley and HoneyPot tools.

Pretrained models have been integrated into continual learning tasks to achieve satisfactory performance levels. However, it's been observed that these models often struggle with tasks that have similar features to previous training data. A key factor contributing to this limitation appears to be the tendency of continual learning metrics to prioritize memory retention over new information acquisition. To better understand this behavior, we examined various combinations of continued training and evaluation protocols on the Mini-ImageNet dataset. Our results showed that a simple baseline protocol, which involves fine-tuning a random initializer without a pretrained model, consistently outperforms the performance of a pretrained model in continual learning tasks. This finding holds true across distinct initialization methods and suggests that continual learning models often settle on a suboptimal solution due to the emphasis placed on retaining memory. Our research challenges the common assumption that using pretrained models is essential for solving continual learning problems and instead highlights the importance of evaluating baseline protocols.

We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space, with respect to a given filament surface, and demonstrate its equivalence to the usual relative homotopy type when working with smooth surfaces and Euclidean space. Building on work by Gromov, we prove that any surface minimizing its area within a given metric space filament surface will be topologically identical to a specific reference surface when the mapping belongs to a particular relative 1-homotopy class. This result is also shown to be a direct consequence of a more general statement regarding surfaces that minimize their area within a given metric space filament surface, and areas that can be expressed in terms of a given function.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data have multiple convergent limits, exhibit distinct behavior depending on whether the limits are equal or distinct. If the limits are equal, we previously established the stability of the corresponding equilibrium solution. If the limits are distinct, we previously analyzed scenarios where the solution converges to an equilibrium or a periodic orbit. This article completes our discussion of scenarios where the solution converges to a periodic orbit by providing specific details, in addition to examining the long-term behavior of solutions whose initial data satisfy higher-order convergence conditions. If the limits are critically stable, we demonstrate that the solution converges to a periodic orbit whose periodic component is determined by a Hamiltonian system with a non-zero constant in the real line. If the limits are doubly stable, we demonstrate that the solution converges to a periodic orbit whose periodic component is an orbit of the Hamiltonian system on the real line. If the limits are singly stable and the solution has an interior nodal point, we demonstrate that the solution converges to a periodic orbit whose periodic component is a non-degenerate orbit of the Hamiltonian system on the real line.
