The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  In addition to OCR, Natural Language Processing, a branch of Computer Science that focuses on human interaction with languages, can be used to further refine the extracted text into a structured format.  This, in turn, makes it easier to validate the ID card when the card holder approaches an operator for assistance.  The study describes the development of an Indonesian ID card extraction tool, which employs both OCR and NLP to extract and validate the contents of an Indonesian ID card.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation methods. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, asteroids with slow rotation velocities are more likely to enter retrograde spin states. Given the YORP effect's cumulative and persistent influence, it is essential to monitor its outcomes on asteroids with known rotation velocities. This study focuses on three asteroids for which YORP-induced rotational changes cannot be reversed in the near future: (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos. Their rotation velocities, determined through light curve analysis, are as follows: (10115) 1992 SK (5.79 ± 0.83 hours), (1685) Toro (5.24 ± 0.07 hours), and (1620) Geographos (1.46 ± 0.04 days). Due to their large sizes, it is intriguing that these asteroids have not entered retrograde spin states as expected from the YORP effect. Furthermore, (10115) 1992 SK and (1685) Toro are the first asteroids for which the YORP-induced rotational changes have been directly observed.

The rise of social networks as sources of political information poses significant concerns about their potential influence on election outcomes. Understanding the dynamics of online discussions on these platforms is, therefore, crucial for assessing their impact. This study focuses on analyzing conversations related to political topics on Instagram by collecting and reviewing 1,500 posts, along with their comments and user interactions. We examined 30 different topics, gathered 1,400 unique comment posts amounting to 57,000 words, and identified 300 comment posts with at least 10 likes or 5 responses. These analyses revealed some comment posts to be highly engaging, even if they went against popular opinions, and showed that users tend to respond to comments from others who share their opinions. We also found that users with more followers tend to post more frequently, and that their posts are often followed by users with fewer followers. This study's findings on the dynamics of online discussions on Instagram may serve as a starting point for further research on social networks and user conversations.

We show that any collection of surface homeomorphisms that is bound in the Röllnik metric does not have compact subcollections. This result extends to collections of surface homeomorphisms that are bound in various other metrics, including the Chabauty metric. This conclusion holds under assumptions that the surface is finite-dimensional, locally connected, and has no compact subspaces homeomorphic to the Cantor space.

Determining stellar parameters for local, faint M-dwarfs is crucial for numerous applications, including characterizing exoplanet host stars. This paper presents a new, publicly available resource for ultraviolet spectral analysis of these stars. By utilizing a comprehensive sample of 539 M-dwarfs, it assesses the accuracy of stellar parameters derived from multiple methods. This includes traditional spectral types, broad-band photometry-based estimates, and results from several empirical and semi-empirical relationships. This assessment is performed for the basic parameters such as temperature, surface gravity, metallicity, and radius. By comparing these quantities to the values required for modeling ultraviolet spectra, this study highlights potential sources of error in the traditional classification of M-dwarfs. It also identifies an inconsistency in the spectral type-temperature relationship for these stars. This resource is a starting point for the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), a comprehensive investigation of these stars' atmospheric properties. This study will provide essential insights into the UV emission of M-dwarfs, their overall behavior, and any variations that may exist.

We propose a novel approach to achieving line ripples at dual metasurfaces in the optical range, and through numerical analysis, we demonstrate the potential for this method to increase the efficiency of ripples in this range. By combining a wedge-shaped subwavelength element with a perpendicular patch at an angle, these structures exhibit highly resistant properties to polarization and incidence angle. When irradiated with coherent light, these structures show a significant ripple effect and a uniform steering capability across different polarizations. The proposed design exhibits a wide spectral range, capable of covering visible light, and can be miniaturized while maintaining its properties. This line ripples structure, capable of being fabricated through standard lithographic techniques, provides a feasible approach for creating line ripples at dual metasurfaces in the optical range.

Although the theory of query evaluation has a long history, our current understanding of its fundamentals is still limited, as evident from the numerous unresolved challenges in the field. This study focuses on a specific aspect of query evaluation – involving self-joins – with the aim of providing a precise difficulty metric. To achieve this, we introduce a new metric, called $k$, which indicates the minimum number of self-join occurrences required to render a self-join query non-trivial. This metric allows us to classify queries into distinct categories based on $k$, which in turn enables us to analyze the inherent difficulty of evaluating those queries. As a result of this study, we are able to demonstrate that several established results can be derived from this metric, while others can be proven using it. Furthermore, we introduce an additional metric, called $d$, which denotes the highest possible degree of integration among a query's tuples. By examining these metrics in conjunction, we can better comprehend the challenges associated with evaluating queries containing self-joins.

Multiple approaches to automating the creation of infinite word generators are discussed, building upon existing techniques such as Rabin's signature and star-free automata, and incorporating various forms of context-free operators, context-free combinations, and B\"uchi-like conditions. The interconnections between these methods and their inherent computational complexities are investigated, establishing that some methods are inherently more complex than others, and others are equivalent to solving deciding problems such as solvability or fillability, and combining some methods may lead to more complex computational problems than others.

The investigation of neutral two-body decays of $B$ mesons offers valuable insights into their transition from a heavy quark to lighter quarks, primarily mediated by electroweak interactions. To gain a deeper understanding, researchers typically analyze the momenta of particles produced in these decays to identify any alterations caused by the transition. To further this understanding, this study focuses on $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ decays to a pair of neutral vector mesons, $K^*$. To minimize systematic errors, a large dataset of $B^0$ decays to $K^\*$ was used as a reference to calculate the branching fraction of $B^0$ decays to $K^*\bar{K^*}$. Furthermore, a significant amplitude variation in $B^0_s$ decays to $K^*\bar{K^*}$ was observed, and the branching fraction for $B^0$ decays to $K^*\bar{K^*}$ was found to be $0.429 \pm 0.064 \pm 0.029$, and for $B^0_s$ decays to $K^*\bar{K^*}$, it was found to be $0.234^{+0.061}_{-0.029} \pm 0.029$.

A recent breakthrough has led to the successful observation of a peculiar phenomenon in the Brusselator system, characterized by a rare occurrence in dynamical systems: the existence of coexisting chaotic and periodic patterns. However, further analysis reveals that this system has multiple variants, including systems with altered reaction rates, differential diffusion, and the Brusselator system itself. This study focuses on the Brusselator system with a variation in reaction rates. Notably, it has an asymmetric layout, featuring perpendicular channels for the species to mix. Despite initial challenges in discovering attractors due to chaotic initial conditions, this study reveals a significant breakthrough in the physics of scattering for the detection of rare events, using a novel method called the "Standard Map with an external force". This approach enables the identification of rare attractors that cannot be found using conventional methods. In the Brusselator system with reaction rate ratios that are neither too fast nor too slow, a novel method was developed for determining parameter values that allow for the coexistence of a periodic and a stochastic attractor. This method involves determining the average flux of species that result from a head-on collision, as well as the time it takes for species to travel the length of their own channel. This time is shown to be linked to the standard map's parameter and can be manipulated by adjusting the ratio of reaction rates. A new bias-corrected estimator has been developed for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the difficulty in estimating it directly.  To overcome this challenge, a bias-corrected estimator has been created by adjusting the standard estimator,  where the standard estimator divides the data into two equal parts based on the absolute values of the predicted values.  This new estimator achieves the best possible bias correction,  as it minimizes the mean squared error of the estimated mean absolute deviation relative to the median regression model.  Some asymptotic properties of this estimator have been explored,  including its consistency and the properties of the estimators for which bias correction is performed.  Bias correction is shown to significantly improve the efficiency of estimation,  leading to a notable gain in the standard error of about $2.5$.  Moreover,  bias correction also facilitates a more accurate evaluation of the predicted values,  which is essential for implementing important tools such as the AIC and BIC.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

Multi-layer Perceptron's (MLPs) have traditionally employed uniform activation functions across all layers. Despite this, recent research utilizing high-dimensional data has achieved notable success by selecting specific activation functions for each network layer. This approach, however, remains inherently linked to the specific application being modeled. In response, our research proposes a novel, adaptable method that integrates varied activation functions into a single, unified framework. Each network layer employs a unique, distinct activation function within this approach. To validate this method, we conducted two separate experiments: one aimed at improving the prediction of mammography samples and another focused on identifying cardiac disease through the analysis of medical records. The results from both experiments revealed our approach yields a significant improvement over uniform activation function MLPs. Furthermore, we found this method to be compliant with the requirements of robustness and generalizability in large datasets.

Animacy, the quality of life associated with animals, has been observed to be reflected in how humans perceive and organize living beings from different species. Recent research suggests the ventral temporal cortex plays a key role in this animacy hierarchy, with studies using behavioral and functional imaging techniques revealing complex hierarchies and patterns of representation. However, the underlying foundations of the animacy spectrum within the VTC remain unclear, with both the simplest and most complex organisms being thoroughly studied while middle-ranking creatures are often overlooked in scientific research. In our novel investigation, we utilized novel functional magnetic resonance imaging data along with novel analytical techniques to dissect the underlying foundations of the animacy spectrum within the VTC. Our findings suggest the VTC organizes living beings along a continuum shaped by two key factors - the complexity of their facial structure and the sophistication of their brain. These discoveries open up new avenues for exploring how humans mentally represent the animacy spectrum, which is a fundamental aspect of human cognition.

The study proves the quantum unique ergodicity (QUE) for Hecke-Maass newforms at a convenient scale, as well as for Landau-Siegel zeros, based on the relative characteristic zero condition and subconvexity.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to allow for the verification of quantum programs with reference to the behavior of other, potentially interactive, quantum programs. Our modification involves incorporating an "expectation" property, which enables the assessment of how a quantum program with relations affects the behavior of another quantum program. This extension of the original Hoare logic is achieved through the addition of an expectation predicate to the basic formulae, and a new set of rules for deriving validity of the expectation property for preconditions and postconditions. Furthermore, we have explored various properties of the derived logics, and demonstrated the applicability of our extension to reasoning about the convergence of quantum loops and the success probability of quantum programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This study investigates how epidemics are affected by super-spreader events in a completely mixed population model. By relating the model to an ordinary differential equation system that represents typical epidemic dynamics, we obtain mathematical evidence demonstrating that a population's overall infection rate can be significantly increased by a super-spreader event. In addition, we show that the impact of a super-spreader event on future epidemic transmissions can be accurately quantified in terms of the epidemic's basic reproduction number. This is illustrated through numerical examples using a susceptible--infected--Recovered (SIR) model and a model with a more complex transmission pathway.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with a cyclic collection of operators, labeled as T, operating on X. This paper explores the spectral properties of the operators within this cyclic collection. Initially, it establishes a connection between the spectral type of one operator and the spectral types of the others. Furthermore, it defines a key operator, referred to as the central operator, and investigates its emission and absorption properties. Additionally, the paper examines the relationship between the cyclic collection's spectral types and the composition of its operators.

The procedure for determining the magnetic field vector in solar regions utilizing inversion techniques has been explained in detail. It was also shown how an existing limitation in magnetic field mapping - bias in horizontal component estimates - arises from the underdetermined nature of the inversion problem and common pre-processing steps in vector magnetograph data. We demonstrate that (1) bias sources can be identified and quantified using a simple analysis of data preprocessing, (2) bias quantification enables a correction step that removes pre-processing related bias, and (3) this corrected preprocessing routine reduces or eliminates bias in the estimated magnetic field components when vector magnetographs with accurate calibration are used. The advantages of this new preprocessing method include magnetic field map comparisons being unbiased and free from pre-determined component bias models. The implementation of this new preprocessing method is also compatible with the current solar vector magnetic field data inversion procedures.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 304 young stellar clusters in 31 nearby galaxies using high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope images from the LEGUS survey. The measured radii range from 0.2 parsecs to more than 10 parsecs, and the majority fall between 1 parsec and 5 parsecs. Under the assumption that cluster half-mass radii correlate with cluster mass, a theoretical line can be predicted to separate bound stars from those influenced by the galaxy's gravitational potential. Based on this model, about 24% of identified cluster candidates lie within the predicted line, while the remaining 76% lie outside due to external gravitational forces. The distribution of projected cluster separations shows a median of approximately 13 parsecs, with a wide range from less than 1 parsec to over 100 parsecs. The cluster separation pattern appears to follow a power-law model with an exponent of around -1.5. It's also observed that giant clusters have a higher average separation distance than their smaller counterparts. However, the effect of cluster mass on separation distance is less pronounced than previously reported in other studies.

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states.

A sign-flipping problem arises in stochastic neural network training, particularly in contexts like matrix factorization and tensor decomposition, where optimization techniques like backpropagation and matrix factorization are applied to minimize a objective function subject to orthogonality constraints. This difficulty inhibits the application of these methods to cubic and higher-order data. To overcome this challenge, a new approach based on complex-valued neural networks has been developed, incorporating a transformation that eliminates the need for explicit sign flipping during training. A modified synchronization loss function is also proposed to facilitate the extraction of a positive semi-definite tensor by transforming the neural network's complex weight matrix. This approach is demonstrated through a series of experiments, showcasing its effectiveness in decomposing tensor data using the Tensor Decomposition Technique. The code for this research is available online.

Prime factors greater than a certain threshold display distinct behavior in their distribution, with a connection to the Dickman $\rho$ function that reflects this distinction. As the denominator increases, the likelihood of a number being a multiple of a specific prime or all primes below it also changes over time. While the probability of being a multiple of a particular prime such as 3 remains constant with an initial rate of one-half, the probability of being a multiple of smaller primes like 2 decreases in the same manner in which the harmonic series increases.

Given any non-trivial free group basis change $\phi$, there exists a bijective mapping $\beta$ that translates words in $F_a$ to words in $F_b$, and a monoid homomorphism $\psi$ derived from $\phi$. For any free group basis change $\phi$, the topological entropy $h_\phi$ equals the topological entropy $h_\beta$ times the complexity of the natural map from $\phi$ to the free group basis change to the natural map from the identity homomorphism on $F_a$ to the identity homomorphism on $F_b$. If $\phi$ is finite and has no loops, then the natural map from $\phi$ to the identity homomorphism on $F_b$ is onto, implying that the topological entropy $h_\phi$ is the product of the topological entropy $h_\beta$ and the complexity of $\beta$.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to give machines similar abilities by enabling them to generalize across tasks without feedback.
A novel method called unsupervised cross-task generalization (UCTG) has been developed, allowing models to learn from related tasks and retrieve relevant information to enhance their performance on unrelated tasks.
Two models have been proposed to demonstrate UCTG capabilities: a basic unsupervised cross-task generalization model and a refined model that includes a contrastive learning component to improve retrieval efficiency.
Through experiments on CIFAR-10 and Fashion-CIFAR-10, the proposed techniques have shown significant advantages over strong baselines in achieving UCTG in image classification tasks.

This research introduces the m-ar-K-Fast Algorithm for Component Analysis, an innovative method developed in partnership with Google that significantly builds upon the previous K-Fast Algorithm. The m-ar-K-Fast Algorithm offers a groundbreaking solution for the blind component analysis problem, enabling the identification of independent components in data sets. It offers a robust alternative to established techniques such as JEDO and K-Fast Algorithm contributions, exhibiting better performance stability and higher accuracy in critical applications where data is heavily corrupted or missing. The m-ar-K-Fast Algorithm's capabilities are demonstrated through practical applications and comparative evaluations with leading techniques like JEDO and K-Fast Algorithm. The proposed algorithm is particularly suited for analyzing large-scale data sets with complex structures, emerging from modern machine learning applications.

This work offers an overview of requirements engineering in the gaming sector.
Existing research studies on this topic have been thoroughly examined.
Key characteristics of the gaming industry were identified and their connections to broader market dynamics discussed.
In addition, several potential areas for further research within this field were highlighted.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that settle the trade-off between privacy and performance, without relying on benchmark datasets, is therefore a significant challenge. The framework we introduced in this paper applies evolutionary optimization to the development of private models. It incorporates the concept of cleanliness to describe data sets that comply with privacy requirements and serves as a model for evaluating cleanliness. Utilizing this framework, we conducted experiments to demonstrate that evolutionary optimization yields models with superior clean performance, both in terms of accuracy and privacy. Furthermore, our research shows that the quality of models derived from evolutionary optimization is consistent across various datasets, models, and scalability levels. These findings provide evidence that evolutionary optimization is an effective method for developing private models of high cleanliness, and this approach may be used to develop algorithms that optimize both privacy and performance.

In this study, we establish a comprehensive boolean structure that is inherent to every group of prime order and associated with a specific partition of its elements. Additionally, this boolean structure is closely linked to the group's underlying architecture, particularly with regards to its subsets of maximal size that are closed under multiplication. Furthermore, we establish that this abstract boolean structure is a key factor in determining the number of elements within the group that satisfy a particular condition related to involutions, despite the fact that this calculation appears at a superficial level.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instruments. The authors of this study analyzed how correlated readout noise affects in-flight measurements for these detectors. By modeling detector noise as a form of time-dependent signal variation, researchers can accurately determine source flux. This understanding will be crucial in optimizing detector performance and obtaining precise scientific data during the mission. This study specifically examines the impact of this noise on the NISP detectors, reveals that it has a daily pattern, and shows that it affects detector performance by introducing scallar and fractional errors. The authors also propose methods for mitigating this effect on flux measurements.

We performed an analytical study to examine the composition of the Milky Way disk using data from the APOGEE-2. The analysis was broken down into two methods. The first approach involved creating a galactic map by categorizing stars based on their latitude and radial position. The second method used a statistical model to remove the influence of galaxy structure on chemical signatures. Both techniques yielded similar results and revealed a correlation between metal content and radial position, with a peak of ~0.12 in [Fe/H] at radii of 6.5 kpc. The model also exposed varying chemical elements among the disk population. For example, there was a scalar relationship between [Mg/Fe] and [Fe/H], while [Ni/Fe] and [Fe/H] exhibited a more complex pattern. The model explained his findings with theoretical models of multiple star formation events. The model suggested that the first significant event occurred with ~11.6±0.8 billion years and was followed by several smaller star formation events over time.

Online rumors pose a threat to public order and need accurate information about their spread and influence. This paper proposes a new approach to assessing online rumor spread and influence based on social network analysis. A specific scoring system is designed to evaluate the speed of spread, reach, and impact of an online rumor. This approach is demonstrated through a case study of COVID-19-related rumors in China. Different social media platforms exhibit distinct characteristics that affect the spread and influence of online rumors. Our results show that some users consistently produce high-quality content, while others regularly post unnecessary information. The score for the COVID-19 pandemic was between 43.16 and 57.54, indicating that the pandemic's influence on China lasted for nearly half a year. Our research provides a theoretical basis for quantitative assessment of online rumors and the COVID-19 pandemic in China.

A novel catalog of 1200 planetary nebulae has been created for the Fornax cluster using observations from the FORNYA integral-field spectroometer. This catalog spans the regions around 41 galaxies within the Fornax cluster and includes multiple objects within the central regions of several galaxies. By employing an Eulerian method to determine distances, a new estimate has been derived for the distance to the Fornax cluster, yielding a value of 19.86 megaparsecs with a margin of error of 1.52 megaparsecs. Additionally, a comparison with previous studies has been conducted, and the density profiles of galaxy halos have been studied using planetary nebulae as a reference point.

This paper introduces LifeStream, a flow processing engine designed to efficiently handle periodic streams. It provides a simple and effective workflow system that can run various types of applications, such as finite-state machines, queries, and machine learning systems. The system has a minimal number of states and maximizes performance by minimizing unnecessary computations, achieving this through a three-tier architecture that includes optimization techniques for data loading, processing, and memory management. Furthermore, LifeStream is a dynamic system that supports online updates, restarts, and resource reallocation to ensure high reliability and flexibility. The implementation of LifeStream is discussed in terms of its scalability and ease of use, and several real-world use cases are presented to demonstrate the system's capability and efficiency. Experimental results show that LifeStream outperforms other flow processing engines and the proposed system is available as an open-source repository.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not require a metric to determine their properties. A specific property, called the bi-associate curve, was found to be a curve's own image when passed through a particular point. This property can be applied to a type of curve called the Bertrand curve, which has specific characteristics that allow it to maintain a constant distance from another curve over time. The study proves that a curve with these characteristics, called the timelike Bertrand curve, can be identified and its properties determined in a semi-metric space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

A new boundary feedback controller is designed to stabilize the Navier-Stokes equations in a rectangular domain, and its stability in a strong sense is proven. Unlike traditional boundary controllers, this controller's effectiveness is not limited to specific subspaces, and it can stabilize the equations in a broad range of modes. Additionally, the controller's performance is optimal within a specific class of controllers.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model divides the material into two separate components - a solid polymer phase and a molten polymer phase - and incorporates the effects of viscosity and surface tension on phase interaction using a user material library within the ABAQUS simulation software. The model simulates molecular level events during strain-induced crystallization, revealing changes in crystalline size and density, and demonstrates its efficacy through simulations of notched impact and drawing processes. The results show the model's ability to predict phase behavior, crystalline size and density, and how they impact mechanical properties.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped FeSe through nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic properties using the full Ginzburg-Landau free energy for multi-orbital systems. The calculated magnetic susceptibility reveals a distinct peak at a low external magnetization strength, which is characterized as a paramagnetic response. We demonstrate that this peak is caused by the interaction of a normal carrier with a triplet Cooper pair, whose formation is facilitated by orbital alignment due to structural strain in FeSe. Additionally, the peak's location can be adjusted through carrier density, thereby offering a method for evaluating carrier density in this material.

The effectiveness of learning-based robotics systems significantly depends on the quality of their supervision. Feedback that corrects mistakes is particularly valuable, potentially allowing the system to adjust its behavior and adapt to changing conditions. Unfortunately, such feedback is often given in a qualitative manner that does not fit into a table and cannot be used to optimize a parameter. Despite its importance, research on using this type of feedback to enhance learning-based robotics has been limited. In response, we investigate a common assumption made by researchers: that qualitative corrective feedback given after the fact can be used to steer the system towards a more accurate path. We demonstrate the potential of quantitative feedback to confirm this assumption and develop a method to evaluate its benefits. Furthermore, we find that these benefits hold across multiple scenarios, including those with moving objects and changes to the environment. Our research suggests that a wide range of qualitative corrective feedback cues can be effective and that their impact is largely independent of the system's initial performance and the difficulty of the task.

Continuous phase modulation (CPM) detection techniques provide coherent and non-coherent performance close to optimal solutions, making them suitable for various applications and scenarios. This paper investigates the water-fading channel and evaluates the performance of conventional differential CPM detection with non-coherent phase estimation. We derive an approximate symbol error rate (SER) expression for the 2-PAM case and confirm it through simulation, also offering a comparison with the optimal differential detector. This analysis serves as a foundation for further study on the modification and optimization of conventional differential CPM detection in various environments.

The interaction between a neutron star and a black hole has significantly more complex dynamics than a neutron star-neutron star merger.  Due to the presence of a strong gravitational well, material can become infinitely stretched and compressed, leading to a sudden release of energy as waves or a shock in space or light.  This process could make these mergers visible in multiple ways, including gravitational wave signatures, a moving shock front, and the resulting neutron star or black hole as the energy is released over time.  The behavior of these mergers depends on the density of the neutron star and the spin of the black hole, and needs to be studied further in simulations that account for the effects of neutron-star core collapse, like the formation of a proto-neutron star or an initial shock.  However, it has been found that the density of the proto-neutron star is the key factor in determining the behavior of the merger, and that it remains significant even after the neutron star has shrunk due to tidal forces.  Mergers with dense proto-neutron stars are found to exhibit a shock-driven explosion, while those with less dense proto-neutron stars do not, resulting in a collapse to a black hole.  The visibility of these mergers also depends on the formation of a shock-driven explosion, and whether a neutron star or black hole is produced, with the majority being undetectable in light.

A previous study investigated the quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility of spacetime using a general class of thermal sources. This study extends that work to all possible source configurations described by the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation, resulting in the determination of the logarithmic derivative of the reduced Wightman function. This derivative corresponds to the compressibility of vacuum states and, in certain source configurations, yields the quantum capacity. The study shows that both the quantum capacity and compressibility can be expressed in terms of the source correlator, specifically the second derivative divided by the first derivative squared. The compressibility is found to be invariant under the replacement of the source correlator with its dual correlator, whereas the quantum capacity exhibits dependence on the specific configuration and cannot be simplified to a universal expression. Furthermore, the compressibility can be related to the ratio of the source's two-point correlator to the power spectrum of the scalar field. The extension to all possible source configurations under the KZ equation also provides a more comprehensive understanding of the holographic principle.

Current deep learning techniques used in removing rain from images have achieved notable success. Nonetheless, most methods are exclusively geared towards rain removal and don't account for rain generation, which means they can occasionally produce flawed output or fail entirely. Our proposed framework dispels this limitation by being a unified model capable of simulating and eliminating rain from images. We've developed a novel disentangled image translation model that separates rain and background images, allowing for the simultaneous generation and elimination of rain. This model is trained in an end-to-end manner using a disentangled image translation loss, ultimately resulting in enhanced rain removal performance when rainfall is intense. Our proposed approach outperforms the competition in rain removal, especially in heavy rain conditions, without prior knowledge of rain intensity.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

The model partnership framework proposes a novel approach to addressing the continuum problem in granular materials. According to the proposed method, the continuum model should be viewed as a means of aggregating information from the bulk for individual particles, rather than a direct representation of particle behavior. This interpretation allows the partnership between the bulk and the particles to be seen as bidirectional, with each component influencing the other. The resulting equation for the bulk density field derives from this two-way interaction, whereas the corresponding fluid dynamics equation would only consider the impact of the particles on the bulk. The model partnership framework provides a clear definition of the required particle-level information necessary for determining the bulk density field, thereby offering a rigorous framework for implementing and testing particle-based models.
This study establishes conditions for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a certain elliptic equation involving Q-curvature on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space.

Recently, the Five Factor Model of personality has been examined in relation to substance consumption, with studies showing a strong link between specific personality traits and drug-related behavior. To further understand the connection, the relationship between the Five Factor Model and the Drug Abuse Screening Test was investigated in this study. Assessing an individual's personality using the International Personality Item Pool Revised Extra-Dimensional Personality Inventory and the Drug Abuse Screening Test, a 150-participant sample was analyzed. According to the findings, personality assessment scored higher in terms of measuring personality traits and drug consumption risk, with the IPIP-NEO-EDX performing particularly well in this regard. Additionally, the results indicated that using personality assessment in conjunction with the Drug Abuse Screening Test in order to predict drug consumption risk was more effective than relying on the test alone.

Human experts typically express relationships between states or actions through straightforward if-then statements, which serve as a foundation for our proposed ATOMIC dataset. ATOMIC details the underlying causes and effects behind various events in society, providing a vast array of situations that cater to diverse contexts and goal lengths. It differentiates itself from other datasets through comprehensive descriptions of causal links, featuring nearly 500 thousands of specific instances spanning 24 broad categories and incorporating inputs from both online sources and crowd-sourced contributions. Furthermore, we introduce the MIOKE dataset, which serves as a more intricate benchmark for our proposed ATOMIC, as it involves crafting intricate if-then statements that capture complex event explanations and incorporate various goals and constraints. We also clarify ATOMIC's potential as a key component for achieving outstanding performance in areas like causal prediction, policy-based evaluation, and human-computer interaction through controlled environments, as well as the potential for further exploring the nuances of human intelligence through various theory-based models.

While quantum computing shows tremendous potential for solving complex linear systems, its usefulness will be limited without a suitable software framework to support it. This project takes a unique approach by examining the performance capabilities of next-generation quantum computers to understand how they can leverage the HHL quantum algorithm to tackle linear systems. Instead of focusing on a single application, this project involves a diverse range of 64 benchmark problems, covering various difficulty levels and problem sizes. In collaboration with IBM and RISC-V based quantum hardware developers, this project involves two distinct simulations of quantum computations, as well as an analysis of the overall performance of these computers when implementing the HHL algorithm. The findings indicate that current quantum computers require numerous repetitions of the algorithm to achieve a given level of accuracy, which is primarily due to instability in the quantum circuit execution. To address this issue, this project introduces a hybrid approach that combines quantum computing with classical simulation, offering significant improvements in performance. The results show that this approach offers substantial time complexity benefits, reaching up to 125 times faster than traditional HHL implementation on quantum computers. The study also identifies potential performance benchmarks for quantum computers, with energy consumption serving as the leading indicator. To support this project, the team has developed an open-source software framework called NISQ-HHL, which is available online.

To enhance data efficiency of speech recognition models, this paper introduces a novel multi-modal training approach that combines text data through a bidirectional attention mechanism. Initially, the system generates text representations from speech inputs, similar to how it normally does during inference. Next, it utilizes these representations, along with the original label-based ground truth, to update the speech representations. This process encourages the model to produce more accurate and speech-related representations during both multi-modal training and single-axis training. Our experiments demonstrate that this method yields significant improvements over conventional multi-modal training methods and existing approaches like bidirectional attention networks and contrastive learning. It particularly outperforms the baseline system in speech recognition tasks with limited data.

This analysis identifies specific areas within a cross section where the average value remains constant, effectively creating a constant average cross section. To accomplish this, a transformation of variables is utilized to simplify the problem and the desired regions are found by examining areas where certain variables remain constant. The proposed method is then validated using an example from physics.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, leading to blocked conduction. The theory of Coulomb blockade also predicts the inhibition of conduction due to the competition between superconducting and electric potential energies. In this study, we examine the coherent quantum phase slip scenario and the Coulomb blockade model by conducting transport and superconducting density measurements in NbN nanowires. Our findings show that the coherent quantum phase slip scenario is not sufficient to explain the blocked conduction, while the Coulomb blockade model successfully recreates the observed data in accordance with the Higgs mechanism. Furthermore, our measurements reveal that the superconducting density varies linearly with applied gate voltage in the blocked conduction regime, thereby providing insight into the interplay between electric potential and superconducting phenomena in these nanowires.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source code for its advanced version, the APOLLO team achieved a comprehensive analysis of existing near-infrared spectra to derive a long-sought detailed picture of this famous T-dwarf's atmospheric properties. This analysis with the code and existing spectral data for 1.5-25.5 um wavelength ranges yielded key atmospheric feature values, including a temperature of 1,030 K, a surface gravity of 4 log(g), and a high satellite population, as well as an initial assessment of its atmospheric molecular composition, which showed a high CO content that may be linked to the object's formation history. This analysis is now the most comprehensive ever conducted for this famous T-dwarf.

Our research offers the initial predictions of the scattering cross-sections for the electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions, based on the quantum field theory principles, specifically within the context of a dynamical quark-gluon plasma. These predictions account for incoming particle kinematics and temperature/coherence lengths, making them applicable to leading, residual and coherent dissociation components of the scattering cross-section. Furthermore, our model includes the treatment of active and observably emitting partons as a whole quark-gluon system, enabling the representation of particle interactions and their internal structures.

Our proposed approach offers a novel view video prediction framework that draws on prior research by Wu et al. and Takeda et al., leveraging both factorization and representation methods. This includes utilizing a factorization technique to predict frame factors, as well as a representation model for view inference. Notably, our model provides a dual representation of the representation method used by Wu et al., incorporating both implicit and explicit features to enhance prediction accuracy. This is realized through the use of a mask-based representation model in place of the one-dimensional correlation model employed by Wu et al. Our model was tested against existing videos in the New Collection and yielded higher score metrics (INDELS) compared to the competition.

In multi-level systems, inter-level coupling plays a significant role in quantum phenomena such as interference and phase shift. However, accurately gauging this effect is complicated due to the need to isolate each orbital's contribution, which is particularly difficult when there is significant direct coupling between levels. In this study, we utilize a novel approach that utilizes circularly polarized lasers to separate space-wise the hertzian components of two co-propagating lasers and directly demonstrate inter-orbital coupling. We observe the result of this inter-orbital coupling in nitrogen when we see that the results of nitrogen being in an air-filled microresonator or surrounded by nitrogen affects the outcome.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches using the same model and also converges them with general particle properties.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our results from a detailed, well-mixed framework to existing research, slight discrepancies were found, which were attributed to differences in cough intensity and breath rate. A validated framework like this has significant implications for creating effective decontamination protocols, as it can identify critical areas where aerosols tend to concentrate, and provide insights into how transmission probabilities could be quantified and predicted. Furthermore, exploring the efficacy of various ventilation strategies within this context could involve collaborating with operational bus network managers. In addition, incorporating the outcomes of such analytical methods into computational tools could facilitate quicker assessment of infection risks in various environments.

Future space-based missions such as QUBES and IACOBA will enable precise measurements of quantum properties in the vacuum, specifically quantum diffraction and birefringence, which are inherent to photons. To fully utilize these capabilities, we must first develop effective detection methods to accurately identify quantum diffraction and birefringence signatures. Here, we examine various detection approaches, including optical systems and potential issues with being triggered by spurious signals, as well as the challenges associated with extracting physical parameters from data sets. A statistical test is also presented to validate the physical model behind these detections and recover the associated physical parameters.

In 1923, J.M. Eisenlohr and G.B. Farris developed a mathematical approach to defining the number of edges in a polyhedron with certain symmetry properties. This approach, focused on polyhedra with the highest degree of transitivity, produced results that incorporated concepts of duality and a specific counting principle. This paper examines the Eisenlohr-Farris Method, exploring its implications and potential extensions to other mathematical structures.

Building upon our previous work, we've developed a novel uncloneable encryption scheme based on the concept of committed messages, ensuring that an adversary creating multiple encryptions from a single commitment will result in those encryptions being identical. Our new scheme expands upon this idea, allowing unauthenticated extensions to be appended to the encrypted data. Furthermore, we prove that our scheme meets the requirements of a strong uncloneable encryption system. Additionally, we explore the first possible construction of a secure uncloneable encryption scheme based on public key encryption alone, without reliance on digital signatures.

This study proposes a novel, keyless authentication procedure for physical layers, specifically for Gaussian noise channels. Based on the statistical properties of randomly generated signals, our approach verifies the legitimacy of a communication session without the use of a shared secret key. We demonstrate that a malicious user cannot deceive the system by presenting a fabricated signal, essentially achieving unconditional security with a relatively low computational load. A computational load trade-off is observable in practice, with larger systems requiring more complex calculations for authenticating the user.

We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials.

This paper expresses the potential function $f$ associated with an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the scalar field $p$, determining when the potential function is constant, and establishing a link between $f$ and $\lambda$. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate.

Both celestial bodies can experience significant mass loss due to an expansive outward flow, which can be driven by numerous mechanisms including intense energy output, high energy transmissions from nearby sources, and internal energy generation. A significant portion of this mass loss can give rise to a absorbing, reflecting, and collisionally heated surrounding space that filters, distorts, and scatters the incoming radiation, shaping the observer's view of the system's spectrum and phase curve. This interacting medium can also impact the host star's or central body's rotation rate by transferring its angular momentum. The flow and the surrounding magnetic field's interaction can result in magnetic connections and pressure differences that, in turn, produce density and density-related fluctuations in the flow. These density differences can cause both the flow to adjust its architecture and the surrounding space to shift its configuration. The flow's internal workings can be studied through the use of diagnostic tools, such as spectroscopy, that provide insights into the flow's microphysics, its relationship with the host star or central body, and the effects of this interaction on the surrounding space.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed an increase in the Bader Factor, confirming an Interfacial Spin-Trapping Effect. These results suggest that the Cobalt/Bismuth interface leads to an increase in Spontaneous Spin-Orbit Coupling, which may induce novel phenomena in the Cobalt layer when combined with Bismuth's strong Spin-Orbit Coupling.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(a,x)=\frac{-a}{r^m}\exp(-br^2)$, where $a$, $b$ are constant parameters and $r=|\vec{x}|$. The potential generalises the Hulthén and Coulomb potentials when $b$ equals zero. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative, solutions are obtained and expressed as $PS$-series. The corresponding fractional boundary condition is established and solutions validated through numerical examples for various fractional parameters in one-dimensional space.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be solved through constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularization. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

Sequential language models are highly versatile, consistently demonstrating success in various tasks such as language modeling, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. Our analysis aims to understand the capabilities of these models with respect to learning the grammatical structure of conflation - a complex word order phenomenon - in Basque. We conducted a series of experiments using long short-term memory (LSTM) models and their extensions, and analyzed their performance in identifying conflation in relation to word order. Our results showed that the accuracy of these models in predicting conflation was similar to that of a rule-based approach, but significantly higher when compared to a control model without the ability to learn relationships across multiple words. Furthermore, we found that the extent of a word's influence on the prediction of conflation varied depending on its position, with a maximum impact of around five to six words. Our research has implications for the design of neural language models and the potential for them to be trained for complex language structures in limited data settings.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow researchers to detect subtle irregularities in the planet's orbit when combined with upcoming observations using the James Webb Space Telescope.

The foundation game Paradox Machine presents a straightforward, effective approach to provide haptic feedback for users, which we found particularly suitable for addressing basic needs in users requiring rehabilitation. By analyzing Paradox Machine in relation to Gelfand and Masse's theory on fundamental human activities, we identified a potential application for foundation games in promoting individuals' physical recovery. Based on this understanding, we designed Reactable RSI, a modular, user-centered version of the interactive surface game Paradox Machine, tailored to meet the needs of patients with repetitive strain injuries during their rehabilitation period. Through the integration of occupational therapy expertise and a prototyping process, we refined the design to make it more accessible and comfortable for users to play the game while receiving therapeutic benefits. Ultimately, our research offers insights on designing more effective foundation games that provide meaningful experiences for users undergoing physical rehabilitation.

This research introduces an energy-based model that incorporates a variational approximation, where a piecewise-rigid map is represented through piecewise affine and continuous approximations in a discrete manner. The model's ultimate goal is to minimize the difference between the original map's energy and the approximate piecewise-rigid map's energy, subject to certain constraints. A significant innovation of this approach is the use of ambient space geometry in the approximation constraints, which distinguishes it from earlier piecewise isometric embedding models that relied on a flat extrinsic perspective. Instead, the new model leverages the ambient geometry to form non-degenerate angles between adjacent pieces of the map, leading to a more flexible and easier-to-compute reconstruction method. Another benefit of this model is the inclusion of fragile regions that are prone to discontinuities, allowing it to be applied successfully in solving real-world problems such as image denoising and super-resolution, resulting in more stable and realistic outcomes.

We investigate how a specific type of vector leptoquark that participates in third-generation weak interactions can produce Drell-Yan dilepton patterns, and to do this, we calculate precise corrections to this process due to quantum fluctuations within the strong interaction, also known as QCD corrections, with the exception of a particular difficult-to-calculate part that is estimated in a different way. Our research reveals that even with quite small masses, the behavior of these leptoquarks can significantly deviate from the behavior predicted by a different type of vector leptoquark that participates in all weak interactions, and this effect becomes particularly noticeable in experiments that investigate high-energy particles and their interactions with each other.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings.

Personalization is ubiquitous in modern technology, shaping what users see and experience. Despite its prevalence, the underlining techniques used for personalization are often opaque, rendering its effects inaccessible to users. This lack of transparency makes it impossible for users to understand how they are being influenced and, more importantly, how their privacy is being compromised. This work proposes novel methods for inferring the personalization and privacy practices employed by websites, enabling the exploration of multiple website behaviors for each user. These methods are efficient, combining the advantages of both model-based and direct observation approaches. By utilizing these methods, we gain a deeper understanding of the personalization and privacy practices employed by websites, as well as the effects of these practices on users. This is demonstrated through an analysis of up to 1,000 participants, with results showing the prevalence of non-privacy-preserving practices and the diverse ways in which users are influenced by personalization. This is achieved through a mobile application that monitors user interaction with websites featuring personalization and privacy policies.

This research investigates the relationship between centering theory and coreference resolution. Initially, we analyzed the interrater variability of coreference annotations using centering theory as a unifying framework. Subsequently, we utilized a set of carefully crafted instances to demonstrate both the potential for a system to surpass human performance and the limitations of current approaches. Additionally, we proposed an augmented training method called centering-enhanced attention, which embeds coreference relations within the context, thereby enhancing the capability of models to handle long sentences. Through extensive experiments on three distinct datasets, our method consistently outperformed the baseline system.

We have developed a parameterized algorithm to determine whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. This is achievable by applying a series of reductions that convert an "yes" instance into an isomorphic subgraph, utilizing a finite set of "anchors" that act as a finite-dimensional projection basis. These anchors play a crucial role in defining the graph's layout. By incorporating edge and vertex properties, as well as specific 2-connected subgraph configurations, the anchor system can be completed, enabling us to solve the Upward Planarity Problem parameterized by the number of edges in the graph. This complements a previously established parameterized algorithm for the Directed Graph Drawing Planarity Problem, filling a key gap in the parameterized complexity landscape.

The growing intricacy of modern computer systems demands considerable time and expertise to set up, recruit, and train multiple components. To accelerate development, a novel automated setup method has been developed, utilizing positive feedback to create optimized configurations. This approach, tested on significant projects utilizing the PyTorch framework, has demonstrated a notable increase in efficiency, surpassing human benchmarks. The proposed technique has been incorporated into an open-source framework called Bonsai, which is now available for public use.

The average growth of a quantum operator is evaluated using simple models, specifically single-site Hamiltonians, which are shown to scale with the number of available states, resulting from either symmetric or finite components. By examining the entanglement entropy growth, a transition from linear to exponential growth is identified at a specific number of available states. A transition in the operator growth rate is found, reaching a maximum at approximately nine available states. This phenomenon is linked to the entanglement transition and a distinction is drawn between it and a similar maximum in the operator growth rate, which instead relates to the number of accessible matrix units.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, is a crucial step often assumed as readily available information. In fact, obtaining accurate distance measurements between these data sets is a challenging problem many researchers have tried to solve. This research aims to tackle this issue by WiFi fingerprinting, utilizing a supervised machine learning model to estimate range distances between collected data sets, specifically focusing on indoor applications utilizing WiFi signals. Our experiments demonstrated that a supervised machine learning approach can effectively utilize signal characteristics to differentiate between various distance intervals, with our proposed model achieving a high accuracy rate of 91.4% for binary classification and 83.5% for multi-classification.

We're taking an unconventional approach to address the ultimate energy crisis facing a advanced civilization. Rather than relying on anti-matter or dark energy, we're exploring the potential of a Dyson Shell to harness energy from a nearby source. In this paper, we consider a scenario where a civilization faces energy shortages and turns to building a Dyson Shell around a Kerr black hole to harness energy from a nearby star. We examine various configurations of twisted, electromagnetic, and pure gravitational fields in the shell's plane and, using the geometric optics limit, determine the advanced civilization's information gain. Specifically, we show that using a Dyson Shell capable of detecting gravitational waves can allow the civilization to detect a Malcom's Cat-like scenario based on observing the shell's behavior.

Network applications rely heavily on service quality, and users often set specific expectations for these services to ensure a satisfactory user experience. Monitoring the status of services and identifying violations of these expectations is therefore a crucial task. This paper proposes a novel approach based on P2P technology that enables users to share trust information with each other. By leveraging this shared information, users can effectively identify SLA violations in a decentralized and user-led manner. The proposed method is efficient, adaptable, and open-source, and the paper provides the architectural framework for the approach. However, further research is needed to fully develop this idea through implementation and validation.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Although the regenerative beam breakup instability is usually the most critical concern, its behavior hasn't been thoroughly investigated for many types of filling designs commonly used in synchrotrons and synchrotron light sources. This paper examines how different filling designs influence the regenerative beam breakup instability and identifies design features that increase or decrease instability risk. Through particle tracking and a macro-particle model, we analyzed various filling designs, including those with interleave charging, continuous charging, and non-uniform filling patterns. The results show that, depending on specific design requirements, filling designs like interleave charging and continuous charging can either increase or decrease the risk of instability, while others have a neutral effect.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems are necessary. One crucial factor in these experiments is the development of sensitive detectors capable of detecting neutrino events resulting from the interaction of neutrons with scintillator sensors, which comprise the bulk of neutrino detectors. Nonetheless, the standard 1D presentation of scintillator data falls short of extracting maximum information from these sensors. By employing a novel 3D-projection method, the inherent asymmetry inherent to the scattering of neutrons on hydrogen can be retained, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of neutrino event classification. In this study, the development of 6-inch 3D scintillator sensors, which form part of the scattering neutron target, is detailed, along with the methodology used for charging, optically clearing, and testing these sensors. Prototypical 3D sensors exhibited an adequate point-response function width, thereby fulfilling the requirements for neutral-particle detection. Utilizing a 365-nanometer LED light source and the 3D-projection analysis method, the standard scintillator response function was derived for the first time, resulting in a measured total neutron cross-section of 34.97 billion bars in depth.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. In all experiments where temperatures didn't exceed 1000 K, we discovered that dry samples displayed increased sticking by approximately 10 times over their water-soaked counterparts. In temperatures of up to 900 K, super-dry samples behave identically to dry samples. Nevertheless, sticking forces in the super-dry samples shoot up to yet another increase of about 100 times in temperatures of about 1200 K. These findings imply that aggregate growth accelerates in a narrow high-temperature range, which may be a critical'sweet spot' for planetary growth.

This R package, lfda, facilitates the implementation of local fisher discriminant analysis (LFDA) across various contexts. The LFDA method is a locally adapted version of the traditional fisher discriminant analysis, tailored to handle datasets with complex structures. The package enables users to execute basic LFDA operations, including dimension reduction, classification, and feature selection. Furthermore, lfda provides advanced capabilities like semi-supervised LFDA, using labeled and labeled data, as well as the visualization of LFDA dimensions. Additionally, it supports the creation of 3D classification trees and interactive dashboards using Shiny. Through integration with other popular R packages, such as keras and torch, lfda also enables the performance of deep learning-based LFDA.
