Additionally, the package is accompanied by non-parametric statistical techniques and a variety of visualizations to ensure transparent and trustworthy results.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained imitation learning, learning from demonstrations in complex environments involves the consideration of various constraints, including nonlinear dynamics, collision avoidance, and complex task objectives. These constraints can be formulated as a robust imitation learning problem with specific modifications to the original demonstration-based learning objective. Current studies have successfully addressed specific subsets of these constraints but have left the general case unresolved. In contrast, we introduce the generalized imitation learning problem (EKMP) which encompasses a wide range of constraints, including nonlinear difficulties and complex task objectives. We also propose an underlying assumption called the learned advantage function (LAF) which facilitates the transformation of the general case into a standard policy optimization problem subject to specific constraints. By doing so, we have developed an efficient solution strategy for our general case, EKMP, which is composed of multiple concurrent optimization processes. We have thoroughly evaluated our proposed solution under various generalized imitation learning settings, including environments with complex objectives, collision avoidance, and varying nonlinear dynamics.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

A novel kind of topological superfluidity characterized by spin-polarized and zero-momentum states emerges in a two-dimensional Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions, where exact diagonalization on finite clusters confirms the prevalence of this phenomenon through various benchmarks. The Rashba interaction sparks a competition between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, which can be adjusted to control the system's polarization. Additionally, by integrating Rashba and attractive interactions, a Rashba-driven superfluidity emerges, which surpasses all possible magnetic orders. A lattice-regularized Hamiltonian formulation reveals that this phenomenon persists in the Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions, where the spin-singlet topological superfluidity emerges when the Rashba and attractive interactions are equally strong.

By utilizing the novel capability of microfocus X-ray diffraction microscopy in magnetized samples, our study reveals the hitherto unknown vortex state transition in the very strong magnetic field limits of a doped La$_2$CuO$_4$-$x$ sample. The examination of three-dimensional vortex clusters reveals an unexpected square-grid arrangement of vortices at extremely high magnetic fields, where the average distance between adjacent vortices is comparable to the London penetration depth. This discovery is explained by the theoretical model of interacting vortices on a continuum using a mean-field approach, where the transition from a closely packed state to an array state occurs due to spatial constraint. The findings also highlight the significance of material properties, specifically the coefficient of magnetic stiffness and type, in determining the structure of vortex clusters.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a new class of models, incorporating a distinct 'exclusion zone' region. Nonetheless, the geometry of this exclusion area on curved surfaces remains unclear. By extending existing theories to account for curved surfaces, our research proposes that the exclusion area takes on an exact geometric shape amenable to analysis through classical polymer theory. Furthermore, we establish a new method to determine the dimensions of this area on arbitrary curved surfaces, facilitating a thorough understanding of brush geometry and potentially influencing the design of block copolymer nanotechnology.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A minimal identifying set is one with the fewest points. We investigate the concept of a trimmed metric dimension, which involves finding the smallest sized set R, after removing a certain number of points from it, that identifies all vertices in a graph G. We provide formulas for trimmed metric dimensions for certain types of graphs, such as rings, toruses, and certain regular graphs, and discuss the difficulty of determining trimmed metric dimensions generally.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image analysis, applying it to all-sky maps created from Fermi-LAT data. The primary objective was to generate enhanced, high-confidence maps highlighting sources that change intensity. The study employed an autoencoder, a type of neural network, to analyze the map data. The encoder compresses the information into a reduced-dimensional representation and the decoder reconstructs the original map. The model was trained to minimize the difference between the original and reconstructed maps. The study showed that machine learning algorithms can create more accurate, source-intensive maps with better signal-to-noise ratio in a shorter time frame compared to conventional methods. However, the results also indicated that training the model with data from machine learning algorithms' sampling processes can lead to decreased performance. The findings suggested that combining machine learning and conventional methods can provide superior results and might be a more efficient approach for identifying variable sources.

In our previous research on monarchical graph families, a key property is that of seriality, ensuring that each subfamily has at most one maximal element. This property allows us to derive an efficient algorithm for determining the minimum number of leaders required to cover the entire graph, by simply needing to identify the highest number of leaderless subfamily structures within the graph. 

Here, we focus on optimizing the coverage using leaders, with the objective of maximizing the number of covered nodes. This problem becomes particularly challenging when dealing with graph structures that contain multiple maximal elements within certain subamilies. 

To tackle this problem, we first explore the concept of binary tree structures, consisting of nodes representing subamilies, with the properties of being in one-to-one correspondence and having no common elements. We then establish the condition for a binary tree to be compatible with the serial monarchical graph property. 

Using this condition, we develop an approach to determine the maximum number of nodes that can be covered using leaders in a serial monarchical graph. This involves identifying the largest subset of leaf nodes within the corresponding binary tree structure, as these represent the subamilies that have exactly one maximal element. 

However, even with the ability to efficiently determine the largest subset of leaf nodes, the problem of finding the maximum size of a subset of nodes that can be covered using leaders in a serial monarchical graph remains NP-hard due to the restriction imposed by the graph's structure. This is because the property of being in one-to-one correspondence introduces

We conducted a comprehensive search for binary asters, also known as Mizar stars, within visual double star catalogs maintained by the US Naval Observatory. Our primary source was the Pulkovo Catalog of Visual Double Stars, from which we identified 136 potential Mizar stars requiring additional photographic evidence. By comparing these targets to historical Pan-STARRS1 images, we were able to discover new evidence supporting the binary asterism nature of three targets, PS1 objects GBL-g.1156, GBL-g.1195, and GBL-g.1213. Our findings have significant implications for the study of binary asters, as they demonstrate that even modern surveys of the sky may miss important celestial phenomena. A quantitative analysis of the effectiveness of combining optical and historical data was also performed to better understand these results.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer influence effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives a new type of the Leibniz Rule for these operators, which was previously unknown. Additionally, examples are provided to illustrate the application of the new rule.

This paper investigates how complex signals are detected using complex data that varies spatially. The detection method employs an adaptive filter based on a minimum mean square error (MMSE) criterion with a fixed number of iterations. We establish a theoretical bound on the minimum variance of the estimated data and show that this bound is achievable asymptotically. The properties of the detection method are examined in scenarios where the signals are distributed freely and independently, and also in scenarios with spatial correlation and fusion. The method is particularly effective in scenarios where the signals exhibit moderate levels of persistence. We further discuss the role of memory in the detection method and the trade-offs involved. The paper is a revised and extended version of the initial work.

We've developed an open-source suite of web tools that utilize JavaScript and the Spectral Characterization Library (SPL), allowing users to create and customize spectral characterizations, update the RCSED empirical stellar population model, and generate model spectra through the use of SEDs. Additionally, this package incorporates elements of the Convergence Framework, enabling multiple lines to be fit simultaneously and incorporating external constraints in the context of the RCSED.

The Southern Atlantic rift underwent a significant change in opening direction over time, shifting from a narrow zone of extension in southwestern Africa to a broader area in southeastern South America. Models of crustal stretching and rift basin geometry were applied across both regions, considering various rates of crustal and mantle stretching. The results indicated that the Southern Atlantic rift experienced multiple periods of slowing expansion, with distinct patterns in opening direction, accompanied by large-scale low-angle normal faulting. These episodes were used to divide the region into four kinematic provinces, whose boundaries corresponded with times of decreased extensional rates. Provinces in the southwest African segment showed wider rift basins and more elevated crust than those in the southeast South American segment due to differences in stretching rates and ratios. In the central African segment, wide, slowly extending rift basins dominated, characterized by high-angle normal faulting and limited crustal thinning. In contrast, the Brazilian segment featured wide, slowly extending rift basins with significant crustal thickening, indicating that this region experienced extensional loading above a stationary mantle plume.

A proven strategy to enhance segmentation models through unsupervised training is unsupervised contrastive learning, which pushes similar unsupervised samples together and dissimilar samples apart. However, this method's effectiveness relies heavily on the quality of unsupervised samples, which are derived from segmentation masks by applying operations such as cutmix and interpolation. These operations, however, introduce boundaries in the unsupervised samples that can negatively impact their representation and ultimately the performance of the segmentation model. To address this issue, this research proposes new unsupervised samples obtained through boundary-sensitive clustering of original image patches, without introducing extra boundaries. The proposed strategy is then incorporated into a self-supervised segmentation framework, which uses both supervised and unsupervised data to train the segmentation model. The experiments conducted on three public medical image segmentation datasets demonstrate the proposed strategy's capability to outperform boundary-ignorant unsupervised training methods, especially when the training datasets are small.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

Similar to other cultural aspects, the meaning of words evolves over time to reflect changing social perspectives. This phenomenon is referred to as "emotional evolution," where words undergo a shift in emotional resonance among speakers. To illustrate this concept, consider the word "adventurous," which was originally used to describe someone fearless, but now is more accurately described as fearless through experiencing novel things. As a result of these changes, existing NLP methods based on static lexical resources may struggle to capture the nuances of evolving word meanings. This challenge is particularly pronounced for applications that rely on word embeddings, which can perpetuate the variations in word meanings through the process of distributional learning. However, there is potential for these variations to be discovered through an unsupervised comparison of word embeddings derived from diverse linguistic sources. By analyzing the variations in word meanings across different language varieties, such as British and American English, or across time, our analysis reveals that words change in meaning at a consistent average rate of 0.016 per year. Our proposed approach, which involves comparing the variations in word meanings across different linguistic sources, successfully identifies 12% of words that have changed in meaning at a rate of at least 0.02 per year. Our code is available for public access.

We propose a new approach to understanding the kinematic dependencies of quasiparticle distribution functions within the context of a nonperturbative, quantum field theory. By drawing upon the Bose-Einstein distribution function, we establish a universal set of functions that incorporate $k_\perp$ dependencies and are tailored to represent the spectrum of particles in a quantum field theory. These functions can be applied to both bosonic and fermionic particles and are connected to the standard quasiparticle distribution functions through specific limits. Additionally, we show that these new functions lead to a more detailed spectrum than that seen with the standard quasiparticle distribution functions and are consistent with the grassmann properties of the fermionic scalar sector of the Standard Model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these new functions result in an irreducible gluon distribution function and an additional gluon distribution function that is $k_\perp$-dependent and reducible.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area of significant interest for biologists and chemists. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach has been developed to evaluate the relationship between these spatial arrangements and the proteins' beta-sheet structures. By analyzing 132 non-trivially knotted proteins, researchers identified 13 distinct bending pathways that could potentially occur in knotted proteins, solely based on their spatial arrangements. These bending pathways were found to be unsolvable in over 80% of the protein knots analyzed. Furthermore, conducting random searches revealed that most of these unsolvable paths correspond to local minima in the energy landscape of the proteins. This finding suggests that the natural state of knotted proteins is one of low-energy configurations and could impact our understanding of protein folding processes.

To address the lingering issue of dark energy, researchers have suggested various theories beyond the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Early Dark Energy (EDE) is one such alternative that has gained attention in recent years. Although initially proposed to begin operating early in the universe's evolution, EDE's properties remain unclear. By conducting a statistical analysis using the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure data, we constrained EDE's parameters. Utilizing a profile likelihood method to calculate marginalization, we derived limits on EDE's parameters based on the assumption that EDE's start time is fixed at $t_{*}=0.1t_{dec}$. Our results revealed the upper limit on the EDE density parameter $\Omega_{EDE}/\Omega_{m}$ to be $0.12$ (confidence level of $95\%$) and $0.16$ (confidence level of $80\%$). Notably, these limits are more stringent than existing constraints, with the $95\%$ confidence level being twice as restrictive. EDE's beginning time is expected to correlate with its density parameter; thus, a more detailed investigation of EDE is necessary to understand the universe's early phases.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is conducted, focusing on its underlying assumptions within a quantum field theory context. The arguments of NG theorem proponents are addressed, and a distinguishing characteristic of the NG bosons that emerges is that it applies only to the case where the symmetry is spontaneously broken in the vacuum state. Further, it is shown that in order for a long-lived nonperturbative sector to coexist with a perturbative sector, the former must incorporate the NG boson and a sector associated with the axial anomaly, in addition to the ordinary fermion zero-mode. The axial anomaly arises as a result of the PCAC hypothesis, specifically through the process of a NG boson decay. A comprehensive understanding of NG bosons is developed, utilizing both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theory theories as examples.

Recent advances in large language models have highlighted their ability to engage in complex language tasks, including the potential to learn from limited guidance in conjunction with extensive datasets. Our research distills this potential by investigating if these models can learn to comprehend phrase-level hypothetical situations through extensive text data. We develop a straightforward, model-agnostic method to evaluate its ability to understand such situations on a large scale. This method enables us to create comprehensive evaluations in multiple languages, along with specialized datasets for English, which are made publicly available for further research. Nonetheless, our findings reveal that current large language models struggle to grasp phrasal hypotheticals correctly, particularly in regards to our observed metrics. We do, however, uncover certain instance types that are more easily managed by these models than others.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs. Our findings apply to the classes of circulant graphs comprised of the integers 1, 2, and 4 when the degree parameter k meets the condition 0 ≤ k ≤ 6.6.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique pinhole pattern, characteristic of super-lateral growth confined by the graphene. By introducing defects into the graphene, it transforms into a remote epitaxial relationship with GdPtSb, demonstrated through high-resolution electron backscatter diffraction and atomic-scale analysis. The study found that misfits between the film and the graphene angle, along with the size of pinholes or domains, can be adjusted through changes to the film's deposition rate, further evidence of a super-lateral growth process. It includes a theoretical model explaining the formation of a metastable state that leads to a remote epitaxial configuration. It suggests that this could involve a critical size of pinholes or domains, required for a Heusler film to find a more energy-stable state on graphene.

This paper delves into the study of $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, initially presented in a previous work where the code's rank and minimum rank distance were examined. Here, we continue the study by investigating its dimension and kernel. Similar to the previous findings, a $p$-ary $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code of rank $n$ can be viewed as a subset of $V_{n,p^2}^{p}$, characterized by equations constrained by the $p$-ary integer combination. The code's dimension is characterized as $d_k=\underline{dim}_k(V_{n,p^2}^{p}),$ where $\underline{dim}_k$ denotes the partial dimension function representing the maximal subspace of rank $k$ contained within the code. Furthermore, the kernel of the dimension function $\dim_{\mathbb{Z}_p} \cdot$ can be expressed as $\bigoplus_{i=1}^\infty \mathbb{Z}_p^{p(p-1)}$ $\cong$ $\mathbb{Z}_p^{p^2 - p}$, demonstrating that the dimension function's entries behave identically to the Fainstein and Talalla's dimension function's entries in $\mathbb{Z}_3$.

The process of injecting polymers into an oil well to enhance secondary oil recovery is a critical stage that greatly affects the final results. To model this process, a combination of flow types (full-scale friction-dominated, laminar, and transitional) is considered in a critical section of the well. In order to minimize the pressure within this section, the goal is to regulate polymer injection over a set period of time. Through numerical simulations, the optimal polymer injection profile is determined by utilizing a computational method that takes into account various types of flow models. In addition, a semi-analytical validation is performed for the transitional flow model, with distinct cases representing different types of well fluids. The results show that the optimal polymer injection profile can significantly reduce pressure within the well, leading to better oil recovery.

A positive label for a sample is designated as the primary target, while additional relevant labels serve as secondary targets. Conversely, irrelevant labels are deemed unnecessary. Existing research focusing on single negative labels has left unanswered questions regarding the sample selection process for multiple positive labels. To address this, we establish a category association network between labels and, through an optimization framework, successfully obtain a desired multi-class classification dataset without direct access to existing relevant labels. Achieving this goal involves solving two computational optimization problems: maximizing the reliability of category connections and reducing the ambiguity of sample assignments. Notably, we leverage only a single negative label for each sample during the process. To facilitate high-performance deep learning, we further propose a novel multi-task architecture that is inherently suitable for multi-label samples. Comprehensive experiments validate our approach, yielding satisfactory results on multiple datasets for both classification and evaluation metrics.

This study investigates the energy bound of a variant of the phase-field equation that has been previously established, specifically the one given in equation (1.3), and demonstrates that it no longer holds no more than $O(\delta^{-1})$ as $\delta\to 0^+$. The energy bound of another modified version of the equation, given in (1.5), however, does still accumulate over time and reaches $O(\delta^{-2})$ as $\delta\to 0^+$. The focus of this research is on the upper bound given in (1.3), and it provides a more restrictive bound that does not accumulate over time and instead reaches $O(\delta^{-1})$ as $\delta\to 0^+$. The proof of this new bound serves as the primary contribution of this paper.

The relationship between physical states and observable quantities is governed by the principle of positivistic efficacy, which can be represented as a categorical relationship that generates a category of physical states (S) from a category of observables (O) through a category of effects (E). This connection can be expanded to involve categories of states and effects that form a subcategory of the category of physical states. These subcategories are characterized by subcomposition and factorization properties that reflect the fundamental principles of positivistic efficacy. This interpretation of positivistic efficacy reveals that physical states possess a composite structure comprising distinct components, each describing a particular type of physical property. This analysis also demonstrates how categories of states and effects can be derived from categories of observables and vice versa, leading to a categorical representation of the relationship between physical states and observable quantities.

The source of very-high-energy gamma-rays in nearby radio galaxies has long been an intriguing mystery. We suggest that gamma-rays are produced when electrons, accelerated by magnetic fields in the galaxy's disk, collide and cause shockwaves that result in the emission of radiation. This theory is supported by the idea that powerful jets in these galaxies are confined by their own magnetic fields, which also restrict the size of their disks. Computer simulations of this scenario reveal that it could explain the observed levels of gamma-ray flux in states of low activity, but it requires that gamma-rays are detected when the galaxy's disk is engaged in a major variation event. The connection between the galaxy's disk and its jet is likely linked, and it is possible that magnetic field variations could cause both restricted jet activity and the emergence of electromagnetic radiation in the galaxy's disk.

This research investigates how portfolio returns are allocated across different stock categories and suggests developing a new method that draws on equilibrium theory. We model this new approach and use historical data to demonstrate its benefits, ultimately creating a systematic method for identifying and sizing portfolio positions. This process is particularly effective at reducing unnecessary risks and boosting potential returns. We also examine the historical performance of this approach in different market conditions and find that it consistently yields better results than existing methods.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate analysis of heart sounds is complicated by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, a new approach is necessary than reliance on noise-free signal processing techniques.  In this research, a distinctive feature extraction method is proposed, based on wavelet analysis, that effectively handles noisy signals by incorporating mathematical expressions for signal and noise properties.  A cardiac auscultation system was developed and tested with 150 recordings from various settings, featuring different types of background noise and the use of several audio devices.  The proposed method was compared to a widely used feature extraction technique, featuring an accuracy rate of 93.33% in distinguishing normal and abnormal heart sounds, in contrast to 90% for the alternative approach.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance, therefore, cannot persist forever, and the chance 
exists that we reside in the universe's first epoch. Our quintessence model illustrates the 
dysfunctional universe dynamics resulting from the descent of heavy states, when a multitude of particles 
are produced, overshadowing the quintessence's power. Additionally, our theory raises implications 
for the universe's early inflationary periods.

The rapid evolution of software applications is generating a substantial amount of interest in the research community, with developers rushing to meet evolving requirements and compete in the software marketplace. While this rapid development creates opportunities for vendors who sell their products to customers, they also face a significant challenge in keeping their software up-to-date with the changing needs of their clients. The problem lies in the fact that, as the size of the software increases, manually identifying areas of compatibility becomes increasingly difficult, making it necessary to automate the processing of software applications. This paper proposes a novel approach to automating the processing of software by introducing a new metric called the Software Complexity Metric (SCM), in addition to developing a method to evaluate software complexity. The proposed approach also includes a complexity-based validation technique, along with a strategy for optimizing the processing of software applications using evolutionary computation. The results of the research were presented at the ICSE 2018 workshop on Evolutionary Software Engineering.

This study explores a complex issue in optimal control theory, where the costs of transitioning between states and taking actions are subject to sudden changes, and we aim to find the most efficient way to switch between different sets of action costs to minimize the total cost. We establish conditions under which a unique policy meets this requirement and proves that this policy can be represented by a set of continuous functions that determine the best action to take in each state. Additionally, we show that this policy can be found by solving a series of linear programming problems.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates unequal leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Unequal production, where leptoquarks are created with different energies, is analyzed and computed at the heavy leptoquark level, then combined with existing research on equal production. In addition, our findings include theoretical predictions for leptoquark decay modes, particularly focusing on the scattering of charged leptons and quarks, and experimentally verified bounds on their energies. Our research builds on previous studies and enlarges the available data, ultimately creating a comprehensive summary to guide leptoquark discovery at the Large Hadron Collider.

This work introduces a novel guided learning approach called SINS, which is designed to model complex time series data of varying lengths across multiple sensors. The approach is particularly useful for predicting unknown time series data based on existing sequences. The primary challenge lies in its high-dimensional signal space, with over 10,000 possible signal combinations, making it a complex task to identify relevant features. The SINS model addresses this issue by learning a low-dimensional temporal representation from a set of sample sequences, allowing it to efficiently predict new sequences. The model is tested on two life science applications: predicting the development of maize seedlings and forecasting blood glucose levels for patients. The results show that SINS outperforms existing methods for these types of sequences. The key advantages of SINS include its ability to handle highly variable sequence lengths and a range of signal features. The work also explores the use of a new evaluation metric called the curve correlation coefficient (CCC), which provides a comprehensive assessment of model performance for time series data. The code for SINS is available online.

We analyze the relationship between the radiation that sparks the [CII] line,
excited by photospheric and neonate stellar radiations, and the excitation of
the CIA line at 492 GHz, also affected by stellar and cosmic radiations. By
focusing on starless molecular cores and low-mass star-forming galaxies, we
evaluate the relative contributions of stellar and cosmic radiations to the
CIA line and find that the stellar radiation generally dominates this process.
However, we also find that the stellar radiation often falls short of sufficient
excitation, and as a result, the CIA line is often underthermalized, with an
average temperature difference of approximately 20 K. This subthermal stimulation may be associated with the observed
deviations from uniform low-mass star formation rates and could be an early
indicator of star formation, especially in large molecular cores. Furthermore,
it offers a potential means to distinguish between starless supercritical cores
and low-mass star-forming galaxies in galaxies' inner regions.

We address the anomalies recently reported in $K$ and $B$ meson decays, specifically involving the processes $K^+	o \pi^0 e^+ 
u_e$, $K^+	o \gamma e^+ 
u_e$, $B^0	o K^0 \epsilon^+ 
u_e$, and $B^0	o \gamma \epsilon^+ 
u_e$. We propose a comprehensive framework to simultaneously explain the anomalies in these decays, making use of a vectorlike doublet with mass $m_\Psi$ that is naturally heavy due to the influence of a strong Compositeness scale $f$. The field $\Psi$ is composed of a scalar and a fermion part, with the scalar part contributing to the anomalous width in a universal manner, while the fermion part is responsible for the decay width. Furthermore, we incorporate the interaction of the field $\Psi$ with the electroweak doublet, achieved through the rotation of the neutrino field and the modification of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix. As a result, the anomalies in $K$ and $B$ meson decays can be explained for any combination of left-handed and right-handed contributions. Through our analysis, we can place a lower bound on the mass of the vectorlike doublet at approximately 578 GeV, given the current data in question.

Levenshtein initially explored a problem involving the sequence reconstruction issue for permutations with the Hamming distance. Given a set of copied sequences of length n, obtained from a unknown original sequence of the same length, the goal is to determine the original sequence. It is assumed that there are at least 2n copied sequences, a maximum of n copied sequences with a single symbol being the same, and a constraint of d being the minimum distance between any two sequences. The goal of this paper is to solve the 1-dimensional sequence reconstruction issue for permutations with the Hamming distance under the constraints of having at least 2n copied sequences and a minimum distance of d between any two sequences. It is proven that if d is greater than or equal to 2, the original sequence can be reconstructed exactly, if d is equal to 1, the original sequence can be reconstructed up to a cyclic shift, and if d is less than 1, the original sequence cannot be guaranteed to be exactly reconstructable.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand its scope, enabling the recognition of a musical instrument from a wider range of categories with only limited training. A novel approach was proposed, building on previous work by researchers Heckkecke, et al. and Wang, et al. It employed a multi-layer hierarchical network to train sub-node representatives and introduced a new protocol called continuous few-shot learning to evaluate models in a more realistic way. When tested against a expanded dataset, the proposed method showed superior performance compared to existing models.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek answers to a variety of questions." What implications does this have for models that rely on datasets with classifications?" For example, what differences would there be between a classifier that recommends relevant papers based on abstracts, titles, and metadata, and one that recommends papers in response to actual queries posed by researchers who have read the papers?" To explore these questions, we developed a dataset called PaperQA, which comprises around 10,000 questions answered by around 50 Ph.D. holders in Computer Science. Each question was crafted by researchers who had analyzed relevant papers. Our experiments indicate that models that classify paper recommendations based on question text and paper features perform significantly better than those that rely solely on paper features. Nevertheless, it appears that cross-checking paper content with question content does not enhance paper classification. Moreover, we discovered that models capable of processing the semantics of questions thoroughly underperform those that rely on shallow linguistic analysis.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform.

We establish that in ASEP, a velocity process evolves according to a specific rule depending on the initial data, and this velocity process is connected to a system governed by the TASEP equation, especially in cases where TASEP's initial conditions satisfy certain requirements.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We examine a Majorana fermion scenario using a Majorana fermion tunneling between two adjacent sites on a lattice, and investigate its behavior within the context of the Majorana fermion-fermion interaction model. This interaction causes the Majorana fermion to exhibit both periodic and aperiodic tunneling patterns. This aperiodic tunneling is a newly identified consequence of the Majorana fermion's non-antiparticle nature. This aperiodic tunneling contributes to the Majorana fermion's density to vary in accordance with a chi-squared distribution. Moreover, we find that the aperiodic tunneling component of the Majorana fermion's density is correlated with its adjacent chiral amplitude, leading to a long-tailed distribution of the amplitude. This aperiodic tunneling also results in the density and chiral amplitude displaying long-tailed correlations similar to those found in the Majorana fermion's density alone. These findings demonstrate that the MFT model exhibits complex behavior as a result of the Majorana fermion's non-fermionic nature.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This platform can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the project's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of laser-induced three-body recombination in gases, specifically focusing on the interplay between electron spin and molecular bond formation. This phenomenon occurs when two same-spin electrons, which would normally lead to electron collisional interference and result in neutral atom production, instead combine to form a single spin-oriented electron in a neutral atom or a polarized spin of two atoms. This outcome can be adjusted by applying magnetic field forces. It is also possible to obtain molecules with varying spin orientations, ranging from ground state to excited states, depending on the relative orientation of atomic spins. This leads to the formation of superpositions of molecular spin states when starting with spin-up atoms. However, creating molecules with complex spin states like manifolds of highly degenerate levels in $^3\Phi_1$ states of Rb$_2$ requires additional considerations of atom-molecule interaction. A quantum regression approach is used to model interactions that lead to spontaneous emission-driven transitions between these high-lying states, resulting in atom-molecule pair creation in addition to molecule formation. This leads to an additional possibility of creating molecules with complex internal states, thus enriching the field of atom-molecule physics.

Our proposed DNA-storage support structure provides efficient support for data organization in hierarchical formats and facilitates point updates, while ensuring data accessibility via sequential search. This support framework utilizes four stabilizing nucleotide base patterns and leverages the asymmetrical properties of cytosine and guanine to differentiate data items and create a hierarchical relationship. Furthermore, our approach incorporates specialized read tools to optimize performance during sequential data retrieval.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention directed network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered images, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that involves approximating visibility considerations through differential visibility computation and parallelization across both brightness and gradient channels, yielding significant speedups compared to current methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to the differential visible-based rendering loss for multi-view image reconstruction, obtaining state-of-the-art results on the widely used DTU dataset while also showing its flexibility in supporting deep learning in other scenarios.

A prominent issue in interlaced video playback is the interlacing effect, which compromises video quality, particularly in scenes featuring rapid motion. Conventional interlacing techniques fall short in such situations due to their limited robustness. In contrast, machine learning-based methods have shown significant improvement in processing interlaced video, including motion estimation and video super-sampling. Our proposed approach leverages a deep learning framework, which utilizes real-time motion estimation to prioritize image processing, primarily focusing on newly exposed pixels. This framework includes two main components: a motion estimation model, which detects changes between alternating frame halves, and a processing model that restores missing pixels based on estimated motion vectors and corresponding pixels from adjacent frames. This approach, incorporating two deep learning modules, has been evaluated on the VSO dataset, yielding superior results in terms of PSNR and SSIM compared to existing methods. Our findings suggest that our proposed technique achieves notable improvement in video quality without compromising real-time processing requirements.

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron density distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a rapid solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three rapid solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a much lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels.
This technique is readily available on smartphones through a feature called HDR.
Although HDR is easy to use, taking advantage of it requires careful consideration
of several factors including timing, brightness, noise and color balance to ensure
the best results.
In order to simplify this process for photographers, a novel approach to
automatically select appropriate exposure levels and fuse images has been developed.
This approach, based on image characteristics and a matrix operator, allows for
efficient generation of optimal HDR images.
In order to verify the effectiveness of this approach, a prototype of the HDR
algorithm was tested and compared to a established method. The results show that
it outperforms the established method in terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics.

Causal learning is a significant direction in machine learning that's gaining momentum. It aims to develop a well-rounded approach by integrating three branches of learning - machine learning, statistics, and economics. Two methods have emerged as particularly effective in causal learning: estimation and optimization techniques. Each has its own strengths and weaknesses, and there are various ways to modify them to suit specific needs. Some techniques can handle latent variables and multi-tasking, while others are more restricted in such cases. Despite these advancements, there are still many challenges to overcome in causal learning. How variables are represented, for example, can significantly impact results. Different representations can lead to distinct views of the data and its relationships. How to select the variables to model another example. There are established techniques for doing this, but there's also a risk of over-adjusting. Then there's the issue of how to model relationships between variables. Different techniques can produce conflicting results, and it's not clear yet how they all fit together.

Achieving uniform and efficient gas-to-catalyst energy transfer in fixed bed reactors is crucial for overall process efficiency.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings within these systems has been a challenge until now.  Our research utilizes the unique capabilities of rapid magnetic resonance imaging to spatially and temporally map the temperature distribution within a cylindrical fixed bed reactor.  While the system is being heated from the sides by an exogenous source, our findings reveal the development of a steady-state temperature arrangement characterized by an inner "hot spot".  The temperature increase is found to follow a linear pattern with depth, despite the cat-alyst's irregular shape, and the highest temperature reading is found at the geometrical center of the reactor.  The presence of a "hot spot" can be avoided by adjusting the reactor's geometry or the method of heat application.  The temperature mapping technique presented in this research provides a precise means of evaluating the temperature arrangement within fixed bed systems.

This note presents a proof for a specific case of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which is based on the $b$-principle and the properties of a family of subfolds within a manifold of dimension one. The investigation into this case reveals that it is a more complicated instance of the Mumford Conjecture, which can be formally stated as follows: Given a smooth subfolds $N$ of dimension two within the complex Grassmannian $G(2,4)$ and a map $f: N \to \bar N$ that is compatible with the symplectic form, there exists a bundle map $F: P \to \bar P$ for some 3-dimensional complex submanifold $P$ of $G(2,4)$ such that it satisfies the properties $\pi \circ F = f \circ \pi$, where $\pi: P \to N$ can be factored into map types I-IV.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation.

The distribution of eigenvalues for realizable matrices with the special structure of non-crossing partitions remains unknown beyond the first row. Despite significant progress made for the first row by M. Shemer in Ziegler's book on flag varieties, the distribution of eigenvalues for the entire matrix with this specific structure has yet to be determined. In our research paper, we make the groundbreaking discovery that the distribution of eigenvalues for realizable matrices with the structure of non-crossing partitions is rational, representing a significant expansion of previous findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of eigenvalues for these types of matrices matches the pattern of an infinite-dimensional classical lattice, such as the partition lattice denoted as P_n.

Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. This taxonomy includes visual material extraction, storyline development, and post-production enhancements to optimize viewing experience. We will also discuss the most commonly employed evaluation metrics, associated datasets, and the advantages and limitations of existing approaches within this field, while exploring promising areas for future research and development.

To assess the perception of security among users, we amply demonstrate a widely-accepted concept using two empirical studies and a simulation. We propose the term "security satisfaction" to describe this perception. Furthermore, we investigate how users make decisions based on security satisfaction in specific scenarios, including choices related to security awareness campaigns and redundant security systems. The findings from our studies and simulation reveal that users often prioritize the reduction of perceived risks over actual risks when making decisions. This insight can be valuable for individuals making personal decisions as well as policymakers and practitioners responsible for implementing and evaluating security awareness programs.

Recently, highly complex nanostructures are being designed on the microscale with electronic and magnetic properties that mirror those of macroscopic materials. However, designing McGratings, specifically pseudo-periodic structures, that mirror the microacoustic properties of certain materials (metamaterials) on this scale is a newer development. We have developed a method to microfabricate acoustic metagratings via two-photon polymerization, allowing us to create structures with multiple layers that mirror linear and curved surfaces. We tested these microfabricated metagratings at ultra-high frequencies and found them to have localized resonance at 40 kHz and 100 GHz. To demonstrate their reflective capacity, we measured the reflection coefficients of different structures, including a flat surface, a curved surface, and one with a defect, and found them to be -14.3, -13.1, and -2.5 respectively. This technique has the potential to also microfabricate metasurfaces and multi-layer microstructures with diverse applications such as sensor development, communication, and sonar system improvement.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between modes in optical resonators and waveguides. The framework is highly versatile, allowing it to address various applications including photonic crystal structures, nanograin suspensions, and microcavity systems. Key concepts such as the linear transformation operator, Hamiltonian operator, and the Kerr nonlinearity operator are defined and their mathematical relationships are examined. Formulations for both discrete and continuous systems are presented and the advantages of representing modes as mathematical objects rather than scalar fields are highlighted. The theory is then applied to examine four specific scenarios: photonic crystal structures, nanogain suspensions, microcavity systems, and optical waveguides.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic stability, enclosing sets, and control policies in systems that can be positively controlled, and we provide converse theorems for linear, affine, and feedback control systems with unbounded controls.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed, high-resolution images from low-resolution images collected by particle image velocimetry (PIV) in turbulent flow. Researchers demonstrated that this method can effectively generate high-resolution velocity fields and associated Reynolds stresses, enstrophy, and vorticity maps at different Reynolds numbers. The model's performance was validated by comparing predicted and actual turbulence statistics, which showed a strong correlation (Raj, 2019).

The paper addresses the ambiguity in the scattering phase shift formula derived from quantum mechanics. It argues that the standard wave formula is uniquely determined by basic principles of mechanics and the underlying structure of plane waves. The discussion applies to both one-dimensional and three-dimensional space.

The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural networks often fall short in this requirement due to their complex decision-making processes. A critical challenge lies in handling open-world uncertainty, which encompasses various unknown categories beyond a pre-defined set of classes. In this research, we introduce a novel, high-performance approach to address confidence calibration in the open world. Our method leverages energy-based objectives to establish a data-driven uncertainty model that learns from labeled and unlabeled data. This approach is characterized by three key aspects: it operates in an open-world setting, is driven by data rather than theoretical assumptions, and is designed for optimal energy-based performance. Our experiments demonstrate that this method yields a significant improvement in confidence calibration across multiple datasets and network architectures. Furthermore, our uncertainty model excels in identifying unknown categories in open-world scenarios.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies.

Understanding business processes relies heavily on process mining, which can be categorized into explicit and implicit process analysis. Explicit process discovery focuses on constructing a specific process model using actual process data, whereas implicit process analysis involves creating a predictive model that uses event streams to estimate a process model. Our research falls into the latter category, where we develop a novel approach to declare a process model implicitly by defining a predictive model that uses event streams to estimate a process model. This approach allows for the exploration of process model and its associated metrics by analyzing the event streams. Our approach and the associated tool, called DeclProcess, are discussed in this article along with an example demonstrating its usage. DeclProcess is available online at [declprocess.alg.ac.uk](http://declprocess.alg.ac.uk).

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths, a phenomenon we term the "reentrant delocalization shift". This occurrence is specifically related to states within the quasiperiodic system's energy spectrum that remain unaffected by the quasiperiodic modulation.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering a wider spectral range and acquiring data at a higher rate, Liger will generate a substantial amount of device data, requiring a more efficient data processing system. To meet this need, we are developing a data processing system that will utilize a field-programmable gate array to optimize real-time data handling, while also creating an interface for software to access device data and settings. This design will provide a framework for supporting Liger's unique capabilities and adapting to any changes to the device or aoNSPIRE software.

Recent research in quantum optics has demonstrated the potential for super-resolving single-photon states through bi-photon spinal mode demultiplexing. This study builds upon these findings and investigates the application of optical systems with angular spatial mode demultiplexing to combine the benefits of super-resolution and high data transfer rates. To achieve this, a model is developed to evaluate the performance of such systems when using optical systems with spatial mode demultiplexing based on angular spectra. The model shows that using an optical system with spatial mode demultiplexing in conjunction with a high-quality factor optical cavity could provide a high data transfer rate of up to 10Gb/s. Furthermore, the model predicts that the combination of an optical system with spatial mode demultiplexing and a quantum backward propagation technique could lead to super-resolution improvements proportional to the number of spectral modes.
This paper expresses geometric moduli spaces associated with certain algebraic surfaces as analytic extensions of corresponding algebraic structures.

In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the specific mechanisms that lead to long-term transient phenomena are crucial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-species ecosystem with a two-timescale structure, where the population interactions are represented by a system of differential equations with distinct time scales. The model exhibits complex transient behavior, and our analysis reveals that certain modular mechanisms are responsible. These mechanisms include a volatile population's rapid response to changes, resource fluctuations caused by a slow-growing population, and the impact of the environment on the population's mean values. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the importance of analyzing the volatile population's early-time behavior and the underlying cause of resource fluctuations in order to understand population dynamics. If the volatile population's early-time behavior is characterized by an asymptotically stable fixed point, then the population converges to a stable average. However, if the volatile population's early-time behavior is instead characterized by an unstable fixed point, then the population may exhibit chaotic or stable infinite-period behavior, and this scenario may serve as an early warning sign for a significant change in population averages.

We investigated the underlying causes of the turning point in the mass-star formation rate relationship, focusing on how the formation of central nuclei affects it. Using a advanced collisionless N-body simulation and machine learning tools to detect central nuclei, we found that their presence correlates strongly with the peak mass of the $M_\odot^{-1}$ SFR function at $\sim 10^{10}M_\odot$. Additionally, we observed that star-forming galaxies with central nuclei have a higher fraction of massive stars compared to those without nuclei, which contributes to the peak in the SFR function. This peak represents the optimal balance between the formation of central nuclei and the formation of rotating galaxy disks, which is influenced by the maximum resolution of galaxy disks formed through gravitational collapse. However, it does not reflect the overall sensitivity of the $M_\odot^{-1}$ SFR function to the formation of rotating galaxy disks.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across different languages, using a shared neural network approach for the tasks. It employs a common representation for sentences from various languages and leverages a shared neural network for the classification tasks. The paper takes a multi-task learning approach, combining tasks such as movie rating prediction and sentiment classification to a single task. It utilizes low-resource language data and high-resource language data simultaneously to a shared neural network model. The paper presents a comparison of different neural network architectures and reveals that the simple baseline architecture is the most effective in predicting movie ratings. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that the application of sentence attention yields better results for sentiment classification. It achieves an 82.5% accuracy on the SemEval 2017 task 1, which constitutes the classification component of the dataset.

Exceptional handling in programs can result in invalidations and downgrades of shared variables, counteracting the efficiency of lock-free implementations. This paper introduces a new technique, combining self-downgrade and self-invalidations to repair fences, yielding a lock-free algorithm for multiple threads accessing shared variables via load-linked and store-conditional operations. The proposed technique can be applied to various lock-free applications, and we demonstrate its efficacy through a case study of multiple threads updating a linked list. The resulting fence repair technique has a constant time complexity and is relatively short compared to other exception-handling solutions.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions.

Consider a fractional Brownian motion $B^{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with Hurst index $H$ in the interval $(0,1)$. Let $f$ be a Borel function from $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and $A$ a Borel subset of $[0,1]$. Conditions will be established under which the image $(f)\circ B^{H}($A$)$ has a non-empty interior or positive Lebesgue measure. This is achieved through investigating properties of the set $A$ based on the quadratic variation $\mathcal{Q}^{H}$ with relation to the SDE $X^{H}$.

Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield predictable outcomes, including the development of quantum disordered states and characteristic H\'enon-Heiles behavior.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with the potential to predict COVID-19 patients' severe conditions. If accurate, using X-ray images for early risk assessment would be a game-changer. Despite significant efforts by researchers to classify COVID-19 from X-ray images, only a few have explored connecting image features to patients' criticality. In this study, we first established a model to accurately identify COVID-19 from X-ray images by integrating Inception-ResNet-V2 and attention mechanisms. This model achieved exceptional performance with an accuracy of 91%, low loss, and high reliability. Following validation of our COVID-19 detection model, we conducted various experiments to identify relevant image features associated with patients' severity. By analyzing features across all classes and using a rank-based selection, we reduced the set to 125 key image characteristics. These characteristics not only significantly contributed to class distinction but also held valuable information regarding patients' criticality. In addition, they demonstrated ability to predict patients' severe conditions, such as respiratory failure and death, with high accuracy. Therefore, these characteristics not only have the potential to predict ICU admission but also other critical outcomes in COVID-19 patients.

The universal simplicial collection is a notable object that has far-reaching implications in the category of simplicial presheaves. By incorporating the universal property of the simplicial set $\Delta^1$, we establish that the universal simplicial collection can be regarded as a simplicial group through a natural isomorphism. This connection provides a significant advantage, allowing the assignment of simplicial groups to simplicial presheaves to be a simplicial functor. Furthermore, this association is responsive to equivalences of simplicial presheaves, resulting in a functor that is sensitive to the simplicial structure.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of erroneous positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives.
