This information is then used to direct the attention of a subsequent forward prediction module, enabling it to focus on areas with previously established mapping connections. By utilizing a memory gate module, EMA-VIO can selectively incorporate past location information into the memory, and a subsequent prediction module leverages this memory to produce more accurate location estimates. Through external memory attention, EMA-VIO achieves state-of-the-art results in GPS-less localization on the EuRoC dataset, surpassing previous GPS-less methods like VIO and GPS-aided visual-inertial localization. Moreover, EMA-VIO demonstrates superior robustness and performance consistency in complex datasets like the KITTI dataset.

Quantum theories describe phenomena where properties like mass, charge, and momentum behave in unusual ways, deviating from classical physics. In 1922, Hermann Weyl formulated a gauge field theory that describes unstable, rapidly decaying particles as they transition between states of different momentum. Weyl's original theory was later integrated into the standard model of particle physics. Building on this foundation, we developed a new framework that expands on Weyl's work, incorporating higher-order processes to better understand the interactions between particles and light at high momentum levels. Our model reveals a novel statistical distribution and demonstrates that exotic particles with unusual properties could exist, exhibiting distinct energies and stability levels when undergoing electromagnetic or gravitational transformations. The characteristics of these particles could be as unusual as indefinite position when momentum is certain or vice versa. Our theory also predicts that particles with these properties could be unstable, decaying into other particles and potentially themselves. Our framework can be applied to describe the behavior of particles in high-energy environments, such as the early stages of the universe.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail.

A federal learning approach is proposed that allows multiple institutions to jointly create a shared knowledge base without exchanging sensitive data. A federal selective collection protocol is developed to aid this process. The proposed method includes a cryptographically secure way to transform encrypted data and a technique for matching queries despite encryption. The federal selective collection protocol reduces the amount of data shared and accelerates query processing. Furthermore, the proposed method is energy-efficient and doesn't require sophisticated cryptographic capabilities. The federal selective collection protocol can be applied to various data types such as documents, numbers, and binary classifications. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through real-world tests using real data.

The entorhinal cortex's grid cell layer possesses a unique neural component that contributes to the generation of spatial grids within this region. This article provides an overview of grid neuron behavior, focusing on their intrinsic properties and the mechanisms underlying their activity. We will examine the roles of grid cells in navigating and their connections with neighboring brain areas, as well as the mechanisms by which their grid patterns are generated, including their responsiveness to animal movement, location, and potential periodic patterns in angular cells' input. Furthermore, we will discuss existing grid cell models and the open questions in this field.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

We analyze the rank of elliptic curves in extensions of the rationals by a quartic field through the Galois group $S_4$ or $A_4$. Our focus lies on elliptic curves with a point of small height in the extension and how their rank increases as the discriminant of the quartic field varies. Our results are based on the distribution of binary quadratic forms in $GL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and how they generate one-skeleton of the genus one surfaces defined by elliptic curves in these extensions. Our findings are particularly applicable to the rational function field $\mathbb{Q}(x)$ and its genus one subfield $\mathbb{K}$, where we establish the increase of the rank of elliptic curves in $\mathbb{K}$ as the discriminant of the quartic base changes.

A holographic system's entanglement entropy growth is governed by the Quantum Null Energy Condition, which is relevant for all conformal field theories. We investigate the thermal dynamics of entanglement in two ways, both centered on the Quantum Null Energy Condition. First, we analyze the change in entanglement entropy for a specific interval of time and find that the average rate is directly proportional to the thermal coefficient and the entropy at equilibrium, which in turn depends on the boundary temperature. This proportionality holds consistently with the Quantum Null Energy Condition, yielding specific bounds on the rate of change in entropy. Second, we examine the difference in entanglement entropy at two distinct temperatures and find that the boundary temperature influences the change in entropy in a way that is in line with the Quantum Null Energy Condition. Both analyses produce similar results and validate the Quantum Null Energy Condition, resulting in specific bounds on the rate of change in entropy, which may be seen as a thermal version of Griggs, Maloney, and Fitzpatrick's argument for the Quantum Null Energy Condition.

We investigate the minimal time required for a qubit state to become distinguishable from a reference state, focusing on the impact of the state's asymmetry. Initially, we establish an upper bound using the asymptotic right-cavity photon number distribution and demonstrate that this bound leads to a more restrictive lower bound. Additionally, we prove that the latter lower bound equals the maximum of two smaller bounds, which correlate the state's distinguishability time with its entanglement and state purity. Moreover, we find that the asymptotic right-cavity photon number distribution is an increasing function of the state's asymmetry, and this relationship informs a more restrictive upper bound for the minimal time to become distinguishable. This new bound surpasses a previously established bound based on the system's energy and surpasses another previously established bound based on the state's puritly, resulting in a more conservative lower bound. However, we also find that this new lower bound can be tighter than a lower bound established through the upper-bound expression.

Given a Hilbert space H and a closed subspace M within it, we discuss the properties of the interpolation projector P_inter, specifically examining its norm |P_inter|, which is our primary focus. It is well-known that P_inter is continuous and maps M onto itself, while on the complement space M^perp, it behaves as a non-expansive operator, specifically having a subnorm of at most 1. We then establish an upper bound for |P_inter|, which is in terms of the smallest closed ball centered on M, and for this, we also derive an alternative expression involving the intersection of M's closed ball with the unit sphere of H. Furthermore, we investigate how |P_inter| relates to 1, discussing both the best-case and worst-case scenarios, which includes demonstrating that |P_inter| can be both exactly 1 and exactly sqrt(2), with the condition that H is infinite-dimensional.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators, enabling real-time observation of temperature variations and potential quantum states.

This study offers a motivic interpretation of curved K-theory for certain algebraic varieties, specifically utilizing a relative version of motivic spectral sequence and identifying a pattern that reflects the geometric properties of these varieties. Our analysis indicates that the motivic curved K-theory spectrum for these varieties is directly connected to the geometric properties, specifically showing that it bridges the difference between the algebraic and geometric versions of these varieties. Our work also establishes a link between the motivic and classical versions of these types of spaces, specifically demonstrating that the motivic curved K-theory spectrum is equivalent to the classical curved K-theory spectrum when looking at these varieties through a specific type of space that is based on fields with a specific characteristic.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over millions of years. To model this, we use a complex system of equations representing various atmospheric processes, including gas exchange between the surface and atmosphere, atmospheric circulation, and plate tectonic activity. At the heart of our model is a system of partial differential equations describing water vapor, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen dynamics. Our study reveals how interior processes, such as volcanic activity and the movement of tectonic plates, influence the atmosphere's composition, while also understanding the role of thermal regulation in controlling atmospheric circulation and heat distribution. Nevertheless, our model struggles to replicate the extreme conditions on Venus, suggesting that key factors are missing. Nonetheless, this work paves the way for a more comprehensive examination of Venus's atmosphere evolution over centuries and larger time scales.

Investigating the interactions between ions and molecules in a quantum system in motion is highly challenging. To address this, we've developed a novel reaction nanoscopy technique that utilizes vacuum ultraviolet light to instantly break up nanoscale droplets of glycol into small groups of ions and molecules while we observe the reaction. By employing this method, we've studied the dynamics of these droplets and found that they've entered a state of quantum coherence. Through further analysis, we've derived a new method for detecting, interfering with, and observing the motion of ions within these droplets. Additionally, our technique has enabled us to study the quantum vacuum better, as it allows us for the first time to directly measure the expected effects of particle pair creation on the motion of ions.

Recent breakthroughs in the evaluation of quantum circuit complexity via matrix product state representations can be build upon to create a practical framework for breaking down these states into elementary quantum gates within popular circuits such as the holographic Hamiltonian and tensor network codes like CSS codes for quantum error correction. This framework involves applying a systematic decomposition process to MPSThe decomposition process involves applying a systematic decomposition process to MPS into a quantum circuit consisting of a limited set of unitary operations, which can then be mapped to a corresponding classical circuit. This leads to a more manageable calculation of circuit complexity and specific code properties. Our research focuses on an efficient decomposition of MPS into a minimal quantum circuit, which we demonstrate through a straightforward application of the decomposition process to notable examples, including the holographic Hamiltonian and various quantum codes, particularly the 2D toric code, stabilizer codes, and the Haah enzyme code. These decompositions, displayed on our website under the category of quantum circuit decomposition, showcase the practical utility of this framework, showcasing which regions of an MPS exhibit highly complex unitary transformations when decomposed.

The success of cancer treatment significantly depends on the accuracy of tumor diagnosis, which often involves time-consuming and labor-intensive processes powered by advancements in computational technologies. Computer vision experts have been working to incorporate artificial intelligence into digital pathology, with many achieving impressive results in classifying biopsy images. However, they often forget that biopsy samples represent just a small part of larger tissues, which are part of organs, and that tumors often develop at various locations within cancers. In an effort to bypass this limitation, researchers have been attempting to construct a unified representation of tissues by combining the information contained in multiple biopsy samples. Yet, as structural systems, tissues have distinct levels of organization, from the fine details of cell nuclei up to broader patterns. Therefore, building a unified tissue representation necessitates organizing the network at different levels of hierarchy. With this context in mind, we propose a novel approach that not only combines the information in biopsy samples but also captures the complex hierarchy present in tissues. Our method enables the creation of a unified representation of tissues by defining a new multi-scale learning objective that integrates the information in biopsy samples and incorporates a top-down mechanism that helps the model focus on detecting objects at different levels of abstraction. To test our approach, we developed a large-scale cancer dataset consisting of over 20 billion pixels and containing over 100,000 cell nuclei across multiple tissue samples, which we used to evaluate the performance of our method on the classification of biopsy images. Our results show that our approach outperforms current state-of-the

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have developed an original Bayesian approach to assessing the model's parameters and their uncertainties, as well as a method to validate the nonlinear Hawkes process model itself. Our technique is efficient enough to be applied to large-scale datasets featuring numerous event types. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through both simulated and real-world data, including research on neuronal activity in monkeys. Furthermore, we explore an interactive web application that allows users to explore a dataset of Twitter posts in relation to various events, such as holidays and weekends.

The development of efficient algorithms for simulations in multiple dimensions poses significant computational challenges. The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) has become a standard technique to overcome these obstacles by reducing the computation time for N-body problems through spatial grouping. The method has been successfully applied in various fields including fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, and general relativity. However, the original FMM formulation lacks conservation of angular momentum, which is a fundamental principle in many physical systems and is often ensured by alternative methods such as the Tree Algorithm. This study presents an enhanced version of the FMM called Angular Momentum Preserving FMM (AM-PFMM), which is a critical step towards developing reliable and accurate numerical tools for the simulation of complex phenomena occurring over long periods of time. The proposed algorithm retains the computational benefits of the FMM while ensuring the preservation of angular momentum and has already been successfully tested in various applications including spinning black hole simulations.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of comparable anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-domain segmentation due to differences in image modalities and organs. In this paper, we introduce an innovative SSL framework that combines contrastive learning and domain adaptation to facilitate training on unannotated target domain images with the aid of labeled source domain images. The proposed framework utilizes a contrastive learning technique to exploit unannotated target domain images and a domain adaptation technique to utilize existing annotated source domain images. We test our method on multiple datasets and demonstrate its capability to reduce the need for target domain annotations during training.

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified theoretical framework based on the Wess-Zumino theory. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated at the 1.5 order level, which significantly complicates efforts to construct a precise nilpotent operator. All attempts to generate a valid nilpotent algebra at the 1.5 order level have been unsuccessful in this analysis. Nevertheless, it is possible to generate a valid nilpotent algebra at the 3rd order of expansion. A key aspect of the associated superfield transformations is the incorporation of auxiliary fields, which are intimately connected with the generation of a nilpotent 3rd order algebra. In contrast, the 1.5 order formalism fails to adequately account for these fields within the superfield framework. A plausible explanation for the apparent success in other approaches may involve the presence of external supertransformations, which complicate the analysis and mask the presence of a defective 1.5 order formalism.

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, there's a growing need to maximize the energy delivered to a target, which can be achieved by converting some of the pulse energy into a polarization component otherwise missed by traditional linearly polarized measurements. This goal can be accomplished by simultaneously amplifying and altering the polarization of the laser pulse in a specific direction, which we show can be accomplished in a magnetized plasma for wavelengths between 1054 nanometers and 1700 nanometers. This technique could enhance the performance of laser-particle accelerators and increase the energy deposited in target experiments.

This note revisits the estimation of the tau electron's electric dipole moment, performing a comprehensive survey of effective field theories beyond MMODD. We carry out a systematic analysis of all relevant operators up to dimension five, using the 2L+G ensemble of complete NLO results in the Standard Model at its natural scale. We demonstrate how the theoretical uncertainties are minimized, eliminating completely the uncertainties arising from NNLO corrections, and incorporating the effects of threshold corrections. We also establish the bottom line estimation of the tau electron's electric dipole moment, regardless of specific effective field theories, yielding a value of 0.026, with a corresponding uncertainty of 0.011. This result exceeds the current experimental limitation set by CDF, and the KLOE collaboration, with an improvement of approximately five-fold.

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis leads to the development of efficient decoding techniques for rank metric codes in binary and extended Galois fields. Specifically, we improve upon existing methods for polar code decoding and introduce new decoding approaches for lattice and quantum codes that outperform the current standard. Our research also enables the creation of reliably decoded lattice and quantum code word pairs, which serves as a crucial foundation for our work on rank metric convolutional codes. This statement has been previously stated on arXiv, posted on 12/20/2021.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. We then extend these training techniques to models that account for foreground contamination, the complexity of which often exceeds our ability to simulate their effects.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson solved a combinatorial problem related to Pontrjagin classes, involving the construction of a combinatorial version of the four-dimensional manifold $M^{4}$ with a specific cohomology ring structure, corresponding to that of the Grassmannian $G_{2}(4)$. This construction allowed them to demonstrate the consistency of the extended Chern-Pontrjagin ring structure on $M^{4}$. Similarly, our work enables us to construct a combinatorial version of the three-dimensional manifold $M^{3}$ with a specific cohomology ring structure, corresponding to that of the Grassmannian $G_{2}(3)$. This, in turn, allows us to demonstrate the consistency of the extended Chern-Pontrjagin ring structure on $M^{3}$.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases.

To increase the effective collecting area of lobster-eye (LE) optics while maintaining wide coverage, using multiple LE units spaced apart is a viable approach. This configuration, termed the multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) arrangement, is particularly suitable for continuous monitoring of sources with moderate brightness. By leveraging the unique pattern of LE projections, MuLE can recover source signals across each individual LE field, enabling seamless integration with telescopes optimized for sensitivity. Based on the characteristics of typical X-ray sources and the capabilities of current LE optics, we believe that the MuLE arrangement can achieve ~10 times the sensing power of a single LE unit, making it an attractive option for its low cost and logical progression from existing LE technology.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To better comprehend the structure of the universe, it is crucial to analyze the relationship between matter and light at its core. Collaborations like the Dark Energy Survey and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey have collected vast datasets, which have enabled the creation of detailed cosmic maps. These cosmic webs, constructed using galaxy positions, reveal the universe's large-scale structure and aid in predicting galaxy distributions. Our deep learning approach, focused on the cosmic speed field's influence on the formation of dark matter halos, has revealed that this field's effects are already incorporated within the cosmic potential field. Consequently, our model has determined that the cosmic speed field's impact on the halo mass function is minimal, whereas other factors like initial conditions and the universe's expansion play a more significant role.

Music transcription, specifically piano transcription, is a complex task with numerous applications, notably in music education and entertainment. What sets it apart from other transcription tasks is the need to capture dynamic relationships in audio data, which comprises time-stamp information. This paper introduces a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization to analyze acoustic data combined with musical notes, with the aim of transcribing piano audio with minimal human input. Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization, an extension of NMF, is a suitable method for this challenge due to its capacity for temporal analysis and feature extraction. Our novel approach builds upon this technique by incorporating note labels as additional columns in the data matrix, allowing for the inclusion of limited annotated data to inform the factorization process. This results in a complex optimization problem, which we solve using an iterative algorithm that takes advantage of the convexity of the NMF objective function. Our method was tested on the MAPS dataset with promising outcomes, demonstrating its potential as a piano transcription tool.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models.

Current machine learning models that extract data from documents require extensive labeling to achieve optimal performance. Nonetheless, preparing documents for training by adding labels to already present information in the documents is a straightforward additional step called "pre-labeling". This process can be time-consuming and costly when dealing with a large collection of documents. To streamline the training process, researchers explored the potential benefits of incorporating partially labeled documents into the training dataset. The documentation typically includes metadata such as the document itself, along with any highlighted areas and attached files. Utilizing a novel dataset that combines partially labeled documents with a wide range of data formats and levels of labeling, the study reveals that models trained on such data perform just as well as those trained on fully labeled datasets. The findings show that models trained on partially labeled documents can achieve up to 5% better performance and 2-4 times reduced training costs with similar performance. The study's success is attributed to the versatility of the proposed approach, which the researchers believe can be applied to other visually rich document understanding tasks.

The observations of neutron star-black hole (NSBH) mergers by gravitational wave detectors hold tremendous potential for understanding the universe's physics and composition. However, enhancing detection capabilities for these events through machine learning-based ranking algorithms requires training models on feature extracts from signal processing software. We've explored training convolutional neural networks using raw gravitational wave signals from NSBH mergers, demonstrating a significant improvement in their accuracy. When compared to traditional machine learning approaches using feature extracts, our method achieves superior results, with an accuracy of over 90% in distinguishing real signals from noise, and notable gains in the false alarm rate and ranking loss metrics.

The social determinants of health (SDOH) play a significant role in influencing an individual's health status, and accessing accurate SDOH information is vital for healthcare providers to deliver personalized care. However, there's a significant gap between the potential of SDOH to enhance healthcare and the current limitations in available data. This gap exists across all aspects of SDOH, including housing circumstances, food accessibility, and language proficiency. To bridge this gap, we propose an innovative framework that utilizes marker-based neural networks to extract relevant SDOH information from various data sources, including text documents and binary formats. This framework can be trained using diverse data configurations, including labeled and unlabeled text, and can be adapted to accommodate a broad range of SDOH categories. Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms existing methods and significantly enhances SDOH inference, while maintaining a good balance between precision and scalability. Furthermore, we've made significant advancements in addressing challenges related to data quality, noise, and diversity, which are common obstacles in real-world SDOH datasets.

This study is centered on a specific optimal control problem related to the movement of a scallop. The scallop's motion is influenced by two main factors: the contraction of its muscles and the resistance from the water. The problem is to determine the optimal muscle contraction pattern that allows the scallop to swim as efficiently as possible. Due to the complex nature of the problem, we take a computational approach, solving the issue numerically for different water resistances using the method of Lagrange multipliers. The study also examines how different water resistance levels impact the scallop's swimming performance.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study used a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It revealed a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis showed that the congregating of already connected individuals contributed to at least a 10% decline in urban diversity. Consequently, our findings indicate that the pandemic may have long-lasting implications for the income diversity of urban settings, emphasizing the importance of promoting physical interactions among diverse groups in urban environments.

Three-dimensional simulations of star formation in a massive (500 M$_{\odot}$) molecular core reveal that the process of accretion and grain growth leads to a significant increase in the growth rate of massive young stars. By comparing their findings to existing theories, the researchers show that the rate of grain growth may be faster than previously estimated, potentially leading to a more efficient formation of massive stars through grain growth. However, further research is needed to understand how massive protostars can maintain a stable magnetic field and create a non-turbulent environment around their orbiting 10 times more massive planetary disk.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've successfully developed a wedge-local net of observables for a class of models that include the massless two-dimensional scalar field and the massless two-dimensional scalar field with a compact spatial dimension, among others. Additionally, we've explicitly derived the statistics of these models by analyzing the Longo-Witten endomorphisms of the conformal net associated with the model's massless sector. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that for the compact case, a modification of Buchholz's approach leads to a consistent description of the field's behavior.

Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower emissions impacting children, teenagers, educational facilities, and healthcare settings. To address these concerns, a systematic review was conducted to investigate the distance between 5G cellular towers and sensitive populations, including children and teenagers, as well as institutions such as schools and hospitals. A second area of investigation focused on 5G cellular tower placement strategies. Our findings revealed that the distance between the emitting base stations and the populations/infrastructure is quite substantial, typically exceeding 200-300 meters. As for 5G cellular tower placement, current approaches prioritize coverage over exposure, resulting in optimization of signal strength while minimizing the impact on individuals and properties near the towers. However, research is needed to settle the debate over the effects of electromagnetic fields on living beings and the environment.

This research investigates how circulation affects weakly nonlinear, surface water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with large amplitudes, varying in time and space, and biased towards right-going waves. We've previously found that circulation influences a specific type of wave, known as the Dysthe wave, by creating a Hamiltonian nonlinear term that depends on the horizontal space coordinate $\xi$ and is derived from a new Hamiltonian formulation. This study extends this by developing a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation to analyze how circulation affects a broad class of nonlinear waves, including those with odd symmetries, and confirms that the new equation applies to Dysthe waves through a simple transformation.

In this paper, we explore a novel approach to studying differential shapes within the context of locally convex spaces. By establishing the Stokes formula for differential forms on differential shapes, we demonstrate the feasibility of examining differential shapes in locally convex spaces, thereby extending earlier research conducted in the context of Euclidean spaces, smooth manifolds, and topological vector spaces.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. These environments evolve over time due to movements of people and objects, which conventional navigation methods find difficult to adapt to. One promising approach to tackle this issue is through the use of sonar technology, which provides critical distance data that can trigger a security-based layered navigation system to adjust its mode of operation. However, the performance of this system is heavily dependent on the sonar sensors' accuracy, which can deteriorate rapidly with increasing distance, thus limiting the system's effectiveness. This problem is addressed in this research by implementing an advanced sonar-fusion algorithm that combines readings from multiple sensors to obtain a more precise estimation of their average distance. This optimized measurement is less prone to errors associated with conventional single-sensor readings, which in turn enables the navigation system to perform more accurately, particularly in scenarios where the sonar sensors' maximum effective range is limited to around 3 meters. The system's efficiency is further demonstrated by its ability to successfully navigate through various indoor environments, even in the presence of moving objects, without the need for a global positioning system.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the bending effect – and develops new methods for predicting their behavior over time. These advances have significant implications for modeling real-world applications such as weather forecast patterns and genetic trait variations within populations.

This research targets addressing the security concerns associated with nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We introduce an encoding method that converts each user's individual message into a unique modulation format. We also develop a decoding algorithm allowing each user to determine the encoding format used. This approach enables users to accurately decode their respective messages despite the presence of interference. We analyze the performance of our proposed scheme and conduct practical experiments using a radio frequency platform. The results indicate that our scheme can effectively prevent unauthorized access and improve reliability in mission-critical applications. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that our scheme outperforms conventional techniques in terms of reliability and Decoding Failure Probability.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an efficient, linearly convergent algorithm using a unique, two-step approach within a restricted domain. By leveraging a direct formula for the optimal rotation, the proposed method achieves significant computational efficiency. Moreover, by applying a tailored technique from optimal transport, the algorithm ensures convergence to a critical point within the restricted domain. Notably, the experimental results show that the proposed method can converge to a suitable solution even without initializing from a neighborhood of critical points.

Emotion-related question annotation is essential for developing effective sentiment-based question answering models, but the process is labor-intensive due to the complex nature of human emotions. BERT-based systems have shown great potential in predicting potential questions, but their ability to handle emotion-related cues needs further exploration. This study focuses on enhancing the efficacy of BERT-based question annotation by identifying relevant cues and developing a method to integrate these cues into the annotation process. A pre-trained BERT-based model was utilized to predict potential question annotations in the EMNLP-MultNLI dataset, and the results revealed that it performed satisfactorily in predicting question relations and appropriate labels. Notably, the BERT-based model exhibited superior performance in predicting relevant emotion labels. The research also introduced an annotation correction tool that leverages BERT to suggest high-scoring alternatives, and the results showed that it was particularly effective in modifying poorly scored answers related to emotion, particularly in cases with subtle or implicit emotion cues. The proposed approach and the annotation correction tool can facilitate the efficient annotation of emotion-related questions by reducing the reliance on human experts.

We explore how societal energy incentives promote efficient behavior in a totally ordered group of individuals, each with distinct energy levels. Introducing energy-based contests that reward the lowest-energy winner, we analyze how these impact distribution outcomes. Our key finding is that, surprisingly, lower-energy individuals have an advantage in such contests, which runs counter to the typical result seen in one-to-one matches. Furthermore, we find that fair contest designs benefit low-energy individuals at the expense of high-energy individuals, while unfair designs instead benefit low-energy individuals through the means of reduced social losses. Through the use of Guilleman's theorem, we prove that fair contest games can be represented by a utility function that is a multiple of the Shapley value, a notable mathematical relationship previously unseen in literature.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct approaches for solving Fluid-Structure Interference (FSI) problems that involve thin structures: a monolithic solution method and a segmented approach. We will detail each strategy's implementation and then apply them to a specific case study, solving the Navier-Stokes equations for a fluid enclosed by multiple thin structures, with a focus on solving a problem with multiple degree of freedom in each subdomain. Furthermore, we will leverage High Performance Computing (HPC) to demonstrate both methods' efficiency.

For autonomous mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective navigation system is crucial. Currently available navigation systems rely heavily on global or local potential fields, geometric methods, or learning-based approaches for path planning. However, these methods have significant limitations when generalized to unknown environments. One major constraint is the need for environmental state knowledge during their implementation. In response to this challenge, a novel navigation framework called HiTMap is presented, which utilizes a unique hierarchical diagram representation called HiTMaps that captures a mobile robot's surrounding space using cylindrical regions. This representation facilitates efficient navigation by enabling the detection of circular boundaries within an unknown environment. The HiTMap framework consists of three main components: (1) a leader module responsible for detecting horizontal lines and constructing an initial map, (2) a follower module that detects vertical lines and refines the map into a HiTMap, and (3) a controller module for managing the robot's movement to follow detected lines. To evaluate HiTMap's performance, comprehensive simulation tests were conducted in various scenarios, including environments with different shapes and sizes, as well as scenarios with moving targets. The results showed that HiTMap enables reliable navigation in complex situations and is resistant to boundary detection errors.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Aggressive Detection Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect aggressive tweets in five target languages (Arabic, Spanish, French, Portuguese, and Russian). For the English subset, we employed BERT-based models in addition to conventional feature extraction with support vector machines, while in the target languages, we relied exclusively on feature extraction. Our reasons for choosing this approach are outlined, along with the features we selected for each language. Results showed that our BERT-based models performed exceptionally well on the English subset, while in the target languages, our approaches ranked second-to-last, indicating there is still potential for improvement in these languages.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

We investigate the emergence of a spin-polarized magnetothermal effect in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides, specifically in the monolayer form of MoSe2, WSe2, MoTe2, and WTe2. These materials exhibit significant changes in thermal conductivity when magnetized, primarily attributed to the diverse interlayer vortex dynamics derived from their unique electronic structure. The magnetic field modulates the carrier distribution, initiating the spin-polarized magnetothermal effect. The considerable enhancement of thermal conductivity upon magnetization can be as large as 100 K2/w in the moiré pattern of these materials. This phenomenon persists even in bulk versions of these materials, where it is driven by the interplay between spiral zones with opposite spin orientations. These findings suggest that moiré materials with twisted interfaces have vast potential for applying magnetic field-modulated thermal conductivity as a sensor for detecting magnetic fields.

We investigate how electron spill-out and quantum nonlocality affect gap-plasmons in noble-metal structures, particularly in the limit where the gap width becomes extremely small. Using a quantum hydrodynamics approach, we incorporate these phenomena and consider their separate and combined effects. We find that the quantum nonlocal response leads to a more significant decrease in gap-plasmon energy than the spill-out does, and this energy reduction becomes more evident as the gap width diminishes. Furthermore, we observe that the spill-out causes a greater shift in the imaginary part of the gap-plasmon energy than the nonlocal response does. Moreover, we demonstrate that both effects combine to result in a more significant reduction in the imaginary part of the energy and the loss factor as the gap width decreases.

Type theory based on intuitionistic, higher-order logic has been normalized through its semantics, allowing the elimination of non-introduction types and the normalization of construction types. This normalization comes with a semantically-based definition of type equality. However, this approach has a limitation: only types with construction properties (product and function types) can be directly analyzed for equality. Other types, such as unit, boolean, and natural number types, have equivalent constructions, but their equality has never been explicitly considered. This work presents a novel method to normalize these fundamental types, thus extending the type equality notion beyond types with construction properties, making the type system more robust and consistent.

This lecture is designed for undergraduate students who have basic knowledge in physics and mathematics. It introduces the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model as a simple representation of topological phase transition and the associated quantum phenomena. We will guide undergraduate students through the calculation of energy levels, wave function properties, and the topological index using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. We will also demonstrate the utility of the model in exploring topological quantum phenomena, including localization, entanglement, and non-reciprocal transport.

In statistics, where data varies significantly, the standard models often fail to capture the complexity of the data properly. This issue is particularly prominent in cases where the data comprises a mix of distinct populations. For example, analyzing financial data might involve distinguishing between fraudulent and legitimate financial activities. In such scenarios, the data likely originates from two or more disparate groups. Therefore, it would be more accurate to model this data using mixtures of different probability distributions rather than a single universal distribution. This paper explores the connection between mixing infinite populations of points in space, where the points follow specific distributions, and analyzing financial data to identify fraudulent activities. It also discusses the benefits of using advanced mathematical theories to generalize traditional mixture model techniques.

We derive the AdS$_5$-only corrections to the two-loop four-graviton superamplitude in AdS$_5\times$S$^5$, confirming the admissibility of this process at two loops and providing a correction to the previously proposed all-order relation between superamplitudes in AdS$_5\times$S$^5$ and flat space. Furthermore, we relate our result to the often-cited "double-triangle" vanishing theorem, confirming it holds for the four-graviton superamplitude at two loops. Additionally, we observe that the cancellation of unphysical poles in superamplitudes relies on the intersection of physical poles rather than the cancellation of the latter.

Recent efforts to accelerate high-level object-based languages with CUDA and OpenCL on GPUs have been hampered by limited memory management capabilities and a lack of parallel memory allocation techniques. As a result, performance is often constrained by slow memory allocation. To overcome this, we present DynaSOAr, a novel parallel memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs. DynaSOAr assigns memory in parallel, reducing allocation time and boosting application performance. The allocator maintains efficient memory access by organizing memory blocks into a hierarchical structure, similar to CPU-based power-of-two systems. We demonstrate DynaSOAr's performance benefits by integrating the allocator into the Java/CLR.NET frameworks and conducting benchmark tests on NVIDIA GPUs. Results show that, depending on the memory profile of each application, DynaSOAr leads to significant improvement, up to 6 times faster than the original allocator, and supports large memory sizes up to 6 GB.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. For a single Mn layer cluster, excellent agreement with experimental data regarding the splitting of the YSR states was found. Additionally, the theoretical framework predicts an antidotted Kermanski plane, associated with the YSR states, located at the Fermi level for a three-atom Mn cluster aligned with experimental findings.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural surfaces to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit neural network, allowing it to adapt and learn new shapes. By exploiting the Fourier series' properties, this approach can predict masks with boundaries of any curvature and even learn multi-object instance segmentation. Since implicit functions operate on a grid based on their occupancy score, FourierMask learns this grid representation through a binary cross-entropy loss on real/fake classifications rather than explicit coordinate learning. Our method demonstrates competitive performance on the MIST dataset, a recently introduced instance segmentation dataset designed to evaluate a range of instance segmentation approaches.

This study examines how a bounded morphism, defined as a continuous mapping between two bounded sets in a higher-dimensional space, behaves in terms of its impact on the underlying dimension. Specifically, it investigates the possible effects on dimensionality when the original set has a particular dimensionality. This investigation focuses particularly on the use of homeomorphisms and variations in the underlying dimensionality when the original set has a certain local dimensionality.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds, which cover approximately 5% of Earth's surface and play a crucial role in global energy balance. Cloud tomography, an emerging field, offers promise in overcoming these limitations by providing detailed cross-sections of cloud morphology. Tomographic reconstruction from multi-angle observations has been successfully demonstrated with data from the MISR satellite for semi-transparent clouds. However, applying this technique to highly opaque clouds poses additional challenges in identifying the "hidden core." We have developed and test an improved approach to recover tomographic slices from MISR and MODIS observations. The core of this approach is based on combining the optical thickness and particle size information obtained from MODIS, which is used to formulate likely cloud responses to incident radiation at various angles. The resulting system is tested using simulated and real data, showing that it is robust and capable of recovering the tomographic slices for highly opaque clouds. The proposed approach can be applied to cloud tomography using data from any multi-angle satellite imaging system.

We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts ion acceleration via a self-induced transparency effect. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which we termed chirped, and how it affects the creation of a dense, charged particle layer with opposite charge to the laser. In this case, the particle layer's charge can be modulated by the changing frequency of the laser, resulting in increased charge if the frequency decreases over time. In our model, ions gain momentum due to their interaction with the electric field of the laser, and we showed that a negatively chirped (frequency increases over time) laser leads to lower ion momentum compared to a positively chirped (frequency decreases over time) laser, given the same initial conditions. Moreover, our simulations revealed that a positively chirped laser can achieve higher ion momentum than a normally incident, unchirped laser with the same power. We attribute this enhancement to a longer interaction time between the laser and particles in the case of the positively chirped laser, causing a greater charge layer and, in turn, greater ion momentum.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune candidates with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the planets' positions and applying the Van Hamaalens method, researchers determined the probabilities of these planets being in the habitable zones of their star, and found that the innermost world has a $7.3%$ chance of supporting life. With an observed spectral type of M3 $V$-type, TOI-712 is a young star suitable for study with other astronomical instruments. Furthermore, considering its relatively short rotation period, TOI-712 exhibits a young star's rotation period that may soon be lengthened in accordance with the Skew Technique.

We investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a method that incorporates large supercells and pseudopotential techniques.  The results showed that carbon defects have no significant impact on the electronic properties but may exhibit local magnetic properties depending on the placement.  In contrast, nitrogen defects significantly affect the electronic properties and may exhibit local magnetic properties regardless of placement.  Furthermore, nitrogen dopants can create localized spin polarized states in the gap, potentially enhancing ferromagnetic interactions.

One potential method for identifying top quark production is through elastic production, which involves observing the effects of the interaction between two gluons in the final state, specifically how they cause a scalar to decay. However, this approach is challenging due to the intricate nature of the process and narrow openings for relevant kinematical constraints. This paper discusses an innovative idea to utilize the unique properties of the vector boson sector to uncover the phenomenon of top quark production. Specifically, it suggests using the relationship between the W and H masses to create a distinct signature that could facilitate the discovery of the top quark through elastic production at the Large Hadron Collider. The plan outlined in this paper focuses on the capabilities of the LHC with its current detectors and requires significant advancement of existing detection methods. Nevertheless, the proposed strategy offers a promising pathway for the discovery of the top quark in the future LHC, particularly in its upcoming high-luminosity iteration.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics.  The X-ray emission lines from iron can be used to study the turbulence within the intra-cluster medium.  However, the conventional approach to analyzing these lines has a fundamental limitation when applying the full shape of the lines to the analysis.  A new method is proposed that utilizes the structure function to estimate the line shape, making the most of high-resolution spectra.  The proposed method is tested under various conditions simulated by random perturbations of initial parameters, and it shows significant improvement over the conventional analysis.  The new method is then applied to a specific galaxy cluster using the XMM-Newton and Chandra observatories' high-resolution spectra.  The results are compared to those obtained from the conventional analysis, and the new method is found to be more accurate, especially when analyzing highly resolved spectra.  The proposed method is a key step in making the most of future high-sensitivity instruments such as the Athena telescope.

An upper dichotomy within the Ramsey property is created by an infinite graph sequence's upper richness, which indicates that regardless of how a specific color is applied to the sequence, there exists a particular pattern that appears infinitely many times. Upper richness can be viewed as a complex version of the Ramsey property. The problem of determining upper richness for arrow relations and various types of tree relations over a specific number of colors has been previously addressed. In this study, the upper richness of cube, star, and square-free sequences is investigated for each color, and upper richness is confirmed for these sequences over two and three colors. No equivalent to the known result about cube-free sequences' Ramsey property is obtained, and a separate analysis is conducted to better understand its behavior. Additionally, upper richness is established for certain sequences that include multiple equivalent edges within a specific pattern, and this result may be applied to obtain upper richness conclusions for combined sequences consisting of arrow, tree, and star relations.

Located within the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation of molecular material. Previous studies have shown that the density of stars in the CMZ has a specific orientation, linked to the galaxy's bar and spherical components. We developed the anisotropic density framework as a mathematical tool to quantify this relationship. By incorporating a two-dimensional correlation function, we refined the framework to accurately identify patterns in the density of molecules in the CMZ. Utilizing radio telescope data from the ATLASGAL survey, we analyzed a specific wavelength range and extracted a set of molecular densities. Our results revealed that the anisotropic density framework is a potent method for identifying patterns in the density of molecules in the CMZ. By applying this technique to multiple regions within the CMZ, we observed that the molecular density is consistently oriented at a 45-degree angle, aligning with previous star density findings. However, our results also indicated a more significant influence from the galaxy's bar component than previously estimated, with a ratio of spherical to bar components of 0.4±0.2. This technique can be further developed for use with other radio telescope data, enabling a comprehensive examination of the molecular structure across the CMZ.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to detect Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Notably, our eye-centric system offers enhanced efficiency and user-friendliness when compared to conventional methods.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d by demonstrating that qudits are more resistant to errors caused by noise when implementing the interaction between particles. This improvement in robustness is even more significant for larger numbers of qudit states. Additionally, we find that in simulations using quantum gates, qudits require less gate application than qubits does, which further enhances the advantages of using qudits. These gains in stability and efficiency can be particularly valuable in large-scale quantum simulations.

Research indicates that positrons are emitted through the interaction of lasers with materials, specifically when taking a thin film target and directing a very intense, circularly polarized laser at it. By changing the angle of the positron detector, research shows that a high density of positrons can be emitted with a specific polarization state, perpendicular to the target and positron detector plane. This emission occurs even when the positron yield is maximized, indicating that this polarization effect is not a result of positron emission being dependent on the angle of the positron's polarization relative to the target. Instead, it's shown that the emission of positrons with a particular polarization occurs naturally when taking the vector potential of the positron as less than one. Additionally, research finds that the density of these polarized positrons can be increased by increasing the intensity of the laser. It's also observed that the density of these polarized positrons can be optimized when taking the focus of the laser to be longer than the thickness of the target. Optimizing the density of these polarized positrons may be crucial in the development of linear polarization detectors.

A group of order m by n (where m and n are positive integers or infinity) has polynomial width relative to a given parameter, indicating an expressible complexity that mirrors that of cyclic groups of comparable size. Under this definition, the width of a group is essentially a measure of its computational efficiency, reflecting the ease with which its elements can be systematically generated using a specific algorithm. The discussion in this paper focuses on finite groups with polynomial width, exploring various characteristics and properties of these groups. The research shows that all finite groups with polynomial width are rational relative to the parameter in question, a characteristic that can result in those groups being isomorphic to a product of cyclic groups, each of a relatively small size that matches the parameter's scale. Additionally, this research demonstrates that the width of such groups is entirely deterministic, taking the form of a product of specific numbers that reflects the computational efficiency of the group.

This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensing unit with a built-in temperature detector, which utilizes a single $56\mu$m$^2$ temperature-dependent resistance element to determine absolute temperatures. The temperature detector's design is based on a bipolar CMOS-IME process and features a minimalist design with only two operational amplifier components. It provides accurate results with a 1.4{\deg}C error margin and achieves reliable readings with a 0.24{\deg}C resolution at a 10.5kHz conversion rate, involving approximately 1.04ns per conversion. Moreover, this design includes a minimal energy consumption of 1.04nJ per conversion, and it offers a compact design suitable for mobile device applications.

Three-dimensional simulations of stars rely on the assistance of magnetic fields to stabilize them, ensuring the proper size. As instability breaks down, the once-axisymmetric magnetic field loses its stability, and a different type of field, called non-trivial, forms. We studied how this new field behaves over time in two areas of the Hertzsprung-Richter gap - near solar-type stars and in more massive stars. By comparing our non-trivial findings to controlled, perfectly axisymmetric simulations, we measured the effectiveness of the non-trivial field in stabilizing the stars. The results showed that even small imperfections could cause significant changes in the non-trivial field, making it difficult to predict how it would behave over time. However, in both the solar-type and more massive star scenarios, the non-trivial field consistently failed to provide sufficient stabilization. Additionally, we found that in both cases, the magnetic energy of the non-trivial field became greater than the kinetic energy of small movements within the star. This could have implications for the maintenance of non-trivial fields in stars through dynamo processes.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve complex problems by translating them into an FRG framework, which involves a set of differential equations that reflect the underlying physics of the system in question. In this research, we introduce an innovative strategy to address these differential equations that leverages numerical fluid dynamics, making it possible to solve a broad class of systems that were previously unsolvable. We test this approach by applying it to a simple quantum field theory, the O(N) model, and present our results in the form of precise numerical data that validates the method. Furthermore, we highlight that our approach holds significant benefits over other methods, such as the ability to tackle systems with non-perturbative long-distance physics. In a future paper, we will expand on this research by examining how the method performs with more challenging systems.

Music notation detection in audio, also known as music source separation, is a critical function with numerous applications, including preserving cultural heritage and restoring historical audio recordings. We introduce a novel interactive approach called Pied Piper to educate AI models about music notation. Built on top of a pre-trained neural network baseline, Pied Piper uses a range of simple interactions to encourage the models to learn about music and improve their performance. To evaluate the effectiveness of this method, we created Quest, a challenging dataset consisting of recordings featuring 13 instruments and covering various environments, making it difficult for the AI to accurately identify the music. By successfully separating music from background noise, Pied Piper achieves outstanding results, outperforming a state-of-the-art baseline model in all categories and successfully separating recordings that the baseline model failed at.

We establish a theoretical foundation for geometric frameworks on Lie groupoids and stacks, building on the work of Kapranov and Voevodsky. By showing that functors of Lie groupoids can be represented through functors of graphs, we demonstrate the equivalence of the category of geometric frameworks on a Lie groupoid to the category of functors from the graph of that groupoid to simplicial spaces. Furthermore, we establish that the category of geometric frameworks on a stack is equivalent to the category of functors from the graph of that stack to simplicial spaces, providing a connection to the broader category of simplicial functors. Additionally, we explore connections between this approach and other methods of representation, such as the use of category theory to describe the homological properties of groupoids and stacks.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass-to-flux ratios, indicating enhanced gravitational pressure that could contribute to the creation of molecular outflows.  Furthermore, we observe a distinct difference in mass-to-flux distributions between protostellar and starless cores, discovering that starless cores with outflows follow a similar mass-to-flux distribution as protostellar cores.  This finding suggests that gravitational force plays a crucial role in initiating the formation of massive stars, and could pave the way for studying the development of massive star formation in infrared dark clouds.

Godel modal logics have proven useful in analyzing theories with introspective axioms, such as reflection, closure, and some provably finite theories. However, the lack of a comprehensive algebraic characterization for these logics poses a significant challenge. Our research aims to provide a universal algebraic framework compatible with Godel modal logics that incorporates relations, building upon the earlier work by Janssen. We first review his findings, then explore how to adapt his results to achieve complete axiomatic characterizations for various extensions of Godel modal logics, such as Grzegorczyk's logic, its extension with the finite model property, and some of its non-normal variants.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms.
